217.text: Wealth in the hands of a genuinely noble person becomes like a tree whose every part turns out to be useful, even medicinal. Nothing about their success goes to waste. For example, a wealthy doctor who quietly funds free clinics turns money into something that heals people far beyond their own life.

218.text: People who truly understand their duty to others don't stop helping just because their own resources are running low. Real commitment to others doesn't depend on convenience. For example, a family going through a tough financial patch might still find a way to share a meal with someone who has even less.

219.text: For a genuinely kind person, real poverty isn't about lacking money, it's the frustration of not being able to help the way they want to. That inability is what actually hurts them. For example, someone who used to donate regularly but suddenly can't afford to feels that loss far more than losing the money itself.

220.text: Even if helping others somehow costs you dearly, that cost is worth paying, because that's how valuable genuine generosity really is. Some sacrifices are worth making without hesitation. For example, someone who takes on real hardship to support a friend through a crisis rarely regrets it, even when it means going without themselves.

221.text: Real charity means giving to someone who genuinely has nothing to offer back; everything else is more like a trade where you're quietly expecting a return. True giving asks for nothing in exchange. For example, giving a struggling stranger a meal with no strings attached is charity, while an expensive gift to a boss before a promotion review usually isn't.

222.text: Taking from others is never truly admirable, even when people try to dress it up as acceptable; giving is always the better path, whatever it earns you or doesn't. The act of giving matters more than any reward attached to it. For example, someone who quietly gives what they can, expecting nothing back, lives a fuller life than someone who's always angling to receive.

223.text: Giving to others without ever complaining about your own hardship is the mark of real character. It takes quiet strength to help while struggling yourself. For example, someone from a modest background who still finds a way to support a friend in need, without mentioning their own struggles, shows what genuine generosity looks like.

224.text: Being asked for help can feel awkward at first, but that discomfort disappears the moment you see the relief on the other person's face. The good feeling that follows outweighs the initial hesitation. For example, someone unsure about lending money to a friend often forgets that hesitation entirely once they see how much it actually helped.

225.text: Enduring your own hunger takes real strength, but it still ranks below the strength it takes to end someone else's hunger. Helping others matters more than merely enduring for yourself. For example, going without to prove a point is admirable, but actually feeding someone who's starving matters far more.

226.text: Using what you've earned to relieve someone else's desperate hunger is the safest place to put that wealth. It's an investment that never really loses value. For example, spending savings to make sure a struggling neighbor's family eats well is wealth put to better use than any amount left sitting in a bank account.

227.text: Someone who's in the habit of sharing their food rarely has to face real hunger themselves. Generosity has a way of coming back around. For example, a family that always sets an extra place at the table for whoever needs it tends to find help arriving exactly when they need it most.

228.text: People who hoard everything only to eventually lose it anyway seem to have no idea what they're missing out on, the genuine joy that comes from giving. Holding on too tightly can cost more than it saves. For example, someone who never shares and later loses everything to bad luck realizes too late that the joy of generosity was there for the taking all along.

229.text: Keeping everything to yourself and eating alone while others go without is actually worse than having to beg for help. Selfishness carries its own quiet shame. For example, someone who refuses to share a windfall with family in need often ends up more isolated than the people they turned away.

230.text: Death is about as painful as it gets, yet even that can feel more bearable than the helplessness of having nothing to give someone who desperately needs it. Watching someone suffer while you're powerless to help cuts deep. For example, seeing a close friend struggle while your own pockets are empty can hurt more than you'd expect.

231.text: Give to those in need and build a life people genuinely respect, nothing else you gain in life matters quite as much. Reputation earned through generosity outlasts everything else. For example, someone remembered fondly for their generosity leaves behind something far more valuable than whatever wealth they kept for themselves.

232.text: Whatever people end up praising someone for, in the end, usually comes down to how generously they treated those who had less. Kind acts are what people actually remember. For example, when a community speaks fondly of someone years later, it's almost always because of what they gave, not what they owned.

233.text: Almost nothing in this world truly lasts except a good reputation honestly earned. Everything material eventually fades or gets used up. For example, money and possessions get spent or worn out, but people still talk about someone's kindness or integrity long after they're gone.

234.text: Earning a genuinely good, lasting name in this life carries a weight that outshines even cleverness or learning on their own. What you build through good character stands out further than mere cleverness. For example, a teacher remembered for their character often ends up more respected, over time, than one merely known for being smart.

235.text: Only truly exceptional people can turn hardship into something that grows their good name, and turn even their own passing into something that cements it further. Their character shines brightest under pressure. For example, someone who keeps helping others despite serious illness, right up until the end, is remembered long beyond their lifetime.

236.text: If you're going to step into something, do it in a way that actually earns respect; if you can't, it's better to sit it out entirely. Half-hearted participation helps no one, including yourself. For example, joining a team just to take up space does less for you than waiting until you're ready to genuinely contribute.

237.text: If people look down on you, the real question to ask is why you're not living in a way that earns their respect, not why they're being unkind. Blame is easier than self-reflection, but far less useful. For example, instead of resenting classmates who mock a lack of effort, it helps more to ask what changed effort could actually fix.

238.text: Failing to leave behind any kind of good name that outlasts you is considered, by pretty much everyone, a real disgrace. A life that leaves nothing behind is seen as wasted. For example, people remember a mentor's guidance for decades, while someone who never bothered to help anyone is quickly forgotten.

239.text: Even the land itself seems to give less when it's carrying someone who never built a name worth remembering. A life without purpose leaves the world around it poorer too. For example, a community thrives around people known for their contributions, but barely notices when someone who added nothing passes through.

240.text: Only people who live without shame are really living; those who live without any good name to their credit might as well not be alive at all. A good name is what makes a life count. For example, someone remembered only for broken promises has, in a real sense, left nothing of themselves behind.

241.text: Kindness is the richest form of wealth there is, since even the most small-minded, selfish people can still end up with plenty of money. Money alone says nothing about a person's worth. For example, a wealthy person known for cruelty has far less real wealth than a modest person known for genuine compassion.

242.text: Look for the right path in life and choose to act with kindness, because however you examine it, kindness is what actually supports you in the end. Every other measure of a good life comes back to this one. For example, someone who treats people fairly through hard times tends to find help coming back to them exactly when they need it most.

243.text: People whose hearts genuinely hold kindness never end up trapped in a bitter, dark existence. Kindness keeps a person's world from turning cold. For example, someone known for treating others gently tends to build a life surrounded by people who show up for them too.

244.text: Someone who protects other living beings and genuinely acts with kindness never has to live in fear of consequences catching up with them. A clear conscience removes a lot of quiet fear. For example, a person known for treating even animals and strangers gently rarely has to watch their back the way someone with a cruel reputation does.

245.text: Genuine hardship rarely catches up with people who consistently act with kindness, you can see it play out all around, everywhere in the world. Kindness tends to attract support when it's needed most. For example, someone known for their compassion tends to find people rallying around them exactly when things get hard.

246.text: People who abandon kindness and make a habit of cruelty are, in a real sense, people who've forgotten what actually matters in life. Chasing gain at others' expense costs more than it earns. For example, someone who tramples over others to get ahead may gain money or status, but ends up losing the parts of themselves worth having.

247.text: Just as someone with nothing to their name struggles to get by in this life, someone without any kindness in them has nothing waiting for them beyond it either. Kindness is what a good life is ultimately built on. For example, wealth might buy comfort here, but only kindness builds the kind of legacy that outlasts a single lifetime.

248.text: Someone who loses their wealth can always work their way back to prosperity someday, but someone who loses their kindness has lost something far harder to rebuild. Losing your character costs more than losing your money. For example, a person who goes broke can recover in a few years, but someone who becomes hard-hearted rarely finds their way back to who they used to be.

249.text: Look closely, and any 'good deed' done by someone without real kindness is as hollow as someone claiming to understand a truth they never actually grasped. It looks like virtue from the outside but isn't. For example, donating money publicly while treating people cruelly in private isn't the virtue it appears to be.

250.text: Before mistreating someone weaker than you, stop and remember exactly how it feels to stand nervously in front of someone stronger than yourself. Everyone is someone else's stronger or weaker in turn. For example, a senior student about to bully a junior should recall how intimidating their own seniors once felt to them.

251.text: Real compassion is hard to claim while harming another living being for food. Caring about others means noticing that our own comfort should not require another creature’s suffering. For example, someone who chooses a meal that does not depend on an animal’s death is acting on that concern.

252.text: We do not truly possess wealth if we cannot protect or use it wisely; in the same way, we cannot claim compassion while choosing to eat flesh. Kindness has to shape our choices, not just our words. For example, a person who speaks gently but ignores suffering when convenient is missing the point.

253.text: A mind that takes pleasure in another creature’s body can become less attentive to compassion, like a person carrying a weapon who stops seeing others as people. What we repeatedly enjoy can shape how we feel. For example, treating an animal’s suffering as entertainment can make cruelty seem normal.

254.text: Compassion means refusing to take life; its opposite is causing that harm and then consuming the body. A caring life avoids turning another creature’s death into a meal. For example, pausing before a food choice can remind us that it came from a living being.

255.text: Life continues when living beings are not killed for food; the verse warns that cruelty carries a terrible moral consequence. Choosing not to eat flesh is presented as a way of protecting life. For example, someone who refuses a dish made from a hunted animal is choosing mercy over appetite.

256.text: If people did not demand meat, no one would kill animals and sell their flesh for profit. What buyers support creates the market that sellers supply. For example, when enough customers stop ordering a product, shops stop stocking it.

257.text: Once we understand that meat is the wounded body of another creature, it becomes harder to treat it as just another ingredient. Awareness should lead to restraint. For example, learning how an animal was harmed can change the way someone looks at a meal.

258.text: Those who see clearly do not want to eat flesh separated from a living creature. Clear understanding can make compassion stronger than habit. For example, someone who learns where meat comes from may choose a different meal.

259.text: Choosing not to kill and eat a creature is better than performing countless impressive rituals. Compassion in daily life matters more than grand displays of piety. For example, quietly sparing an animal shows more mercy than making a public show of devotion while causing harm.

260.text: All living beings honor the person who neither kills them nor eats them. Respect for life earns a kind of trust that no speech can command. For example, an animal treated gently is safer around a person who never harms it.

261.text: The heart of disciplined living is bearing our own hardship without causing pain to another living being. Endurance matters only when it is joined with harmlessness. For example, staying calm through a difficult training session without taking frustration out on a teammate is a small form of this discipline.

262.text: Self-discipline belongs to people who genuinely live by it; simply wearing the image of an ascetic achieves nothing. A strict appearance cannot replace inner control. For example, calling yourself disciplined while giving up whenever work becomes difficult fools no one for long.

263.text: People should not forget their own practice of self-control merely because they want to support those who have renounced ordinary life. Helping others is good, but it does not excuse neglecting our own duties. For example, donating to a good cause while refusing to control harmful habits leaves the work unfinished.

264.text: Deep self-discipline gives a person the strength to overcome hostility and strengthen good relationships. Inner control can change both conflict and friendship. For example, someone who stays steady during an argument may calm an enemy and win back a friend.

265.text: Serious self-discipline is valued because it helps people reach what they truly seek. Focused effort can turn a wish into an achievement. For example, a student who follows a demanding study plan is more likely to reach a difficult goal.

266.text: Those who practice self-control are doing the work that truly belongs to them; people ruled by desire waste their effort. Discipline directs energy, while unchecked craving scatters it. For example, finishing an important assignment instead of endlessly chasing distractions is a practical form of this lesson.

267.text: Gold becomes brighter in the fire, and a disciplined person can become stronger through hardship. Difficulties can deepen wisdom when we face them with purpose. For example, an athlete who learns from exhausting training may emerge more capable and confident.

268.text: The person who lets go of ego and possessiveness earns the respect of other living beings. Greatness grows when someone stops making everything about “me” and “mine.” For example, a leader who shares credit and listens to others is respected more than one who demands praise.

269.text: Those who gain the full strength of self-discipline can face even the fear of death. Their courage is not the absence of danger but mastery over panic. For example, a person who remains brave and purposeful during a serious crisis shows this strength.

270.text: There are many people who feel powerless because only a few practice the discipline that builds real strength. Self-control is uncommon, but its absence leaves people vulnerable to every desire. For example, a group with many impulsive members but few steady leaders quickly loses direction.

271.text: A dishonest person who pretends to be virtuous cannot hide the truth from himself; it is as if the very elements of his body were laughing at the act. False goodness is still deception. For example, someone who posts about integrity while cheating in private eventually exposes the gap.

272.text: A lofty spiritual appearance means nothing if a person knowingly keeps doing what their own conscience calls wrong. Outer status cannot erase inner guilt. For example, a respected volunteer who secretly harms others is not made virtuous by their public image.

273.text: A person who cannot control the mind but wears a powerful spiritual image is like a cow hiding under a tiger skin while grazing. Appearance can frighten or impress people, but it does not change what is underneath. For example, acting tough or holy while giving in to every impulse is only a disguise.

274.text: Using an ascetic appearance to commit wrongdoing is like a hunter hiding in a bush to trap birds. A respected role becomes especially harmful when it is used to ambush trust. For example, someone who poses as a helpful adviser only to exploit people is using a disguise as a trap.

275.text: People who claim to have given up attachment but live deceitfully will eventually suffer deep regret. Pretending to be detached does not protect anyone from the results of dishonest choices. For example, a person who lies about being above money may later lose friends and ask why they acted that way.

276.text: Few people are harder-hearted than those who keep their desires inside but pretend to have renounced them. Hidden selfishness can make deception especially cruel. For example, a manager who acts selfless while secretly taking every benefit for themselves abuses the trust of the team.

277.text: Some people look bright and respectable on the outside but carry a dark heart within, like a red berry with a black tip. Appearance alone is not proof of character. For example, a charming classmate may seem kind until their private actions reveal deliberate cruelty.

278.text: Many people hide a polluted mind behind clean clothes, rituals, or an impressive reputation. Looking pure does not make a person pure. For example, someone may speak about virtue at a ceremony while bullying others afterward.

279.text: An arrow looks straight but is used to harm, while a curved lute creates beautiful music; judge people by what they do, not how they look. Shape and style can mislead us. For example, a quiet applicant who works honestly may be more trustworthy than a polished speaker who breaks promises.

280.text: A shaved head, long hair, or any other outward sign is unnecessary if a person truly leaves behind the conduct that wise people reject. Real renunciation is shown in behavior, not costume. For example, someone who gives up cruelty and dishonesty needs no special appearance to prove their change.

281.text: Anyone who wants to avoid disgrace must guard the mind against wanting what belongs to someone else. Integrity begins before the hand reaches for anything. For example, refusing to copy a classmate’s work protects both their effort and your own reputation.

282.text: Even planning to secretly take another person’s property is already a moral failure. Wrongdoing begins in the mind before it appears in action. For example, deciding how to use a friend’s password without permission is wrong even if you never log in.

283.text: Wealth gained by theft may seem to grow at first, but it eventually destroys itself. Dishonest gain carries fear, loss, and consequences within it. For example, money stolen from a business can lead to dismissal, legal trouble, and the loss of trust that money cannot repair.

284.text: A strong desire to steal brings lasting pain when its consequences arrive. The thrill of getting something quickly cannot cancel the damage it causes. For example, taking a phone may seem like an easy win until guilt, fear, and the victim’s loss follow you.

285.text: Someone who watches for another person’s careless moment to steal cannot at the same time claim to be guided by kindness. Compassion does not wait for weakness to exploit. For example, taking a roommate’s money while they are distracted reveals what matters more than polite words.

286.text: People who strongly desire to defraud others cannot live by fair limits and honest restraint. Greed keeps pushing them beyond what is enough. For example, a seller who keeps hiding defects to make extra money cannot honestly say they respect fair dealing.

287.text: The dark cleverness used for theft cannot live in someone who values measured, honorable living. A person who respects limits has no need for deceptive shortcuts. For example, someone who budgets carefully is less likely to manipulate others for money.

288.text: Honesty settles in the heart of a fair-minded person, while deceit settles in the heart of someone practiced in theft. Repeated choices shape character. For example, a student who regularly cheats becomes secretive, while one who works honestly grows more dependable.

289.text: People who know no way to succeed except through theft can ruin themselves in the very act of breaking the rules. A dishonest habit eventually becomes its own downfall. For example, an employee who falsifies records may lose a career built over many years.

290.text: Even worldly security can slip away from a thief, while honest conduct does not close the door to a better life. A person who refuses fraud protects both present trust and future hope. For example, a worker trusted with money keeps that trust by refusing to take even a small amount.

291.text: Truth means speaking words that do no harm. Accuracy matters, but truth should not be used as an excuse to injure people. For example, giving honest feedback kindly helps someone improve without humiliating them.

292.text: A statement that is not literally true may still be treated as truthful when it brings completely blameless good. This is a narrow exception, not a license to lie for convenience. For example, a surprise planned to comfort someone can hide the truth without harming anyone.

293.text: Do not say what your own conscience knows is false, because the lie will keep burning inside you afterward. Guilt can become its own punishment. For example, blaming a teammate for your mistake may fool others briefly, but you still have to live with knowing the truth.

294.text: A person who lives without lying even in their own heart earns a lasting place in people’s respect. Trust grows when words and private actions match. For example, a friend who tells the truth even when it is embarrassing becomes someone others can rely on.

295.text: Speaking truth sincerely from the heart is higher than performing great acts without honesty. Character in ordinary speech can matter more than impressive religious or charitable displays. For example, admitting a mistake openly may show more virtue than making a public donation for praise.

296.text: No reputation is greater than being known as someone who does not lie, and that honesty supports every other virtue. Truthfulness quietly shapes the rest of a person’s life. For example, an honest teammate becomes trusted with responsibility because people know their word is dependable.

297.text: If a person can truly avoid falsehood, that achievement is so valuable that even the absence of other virtues is less troubling. Honesty is a foundation from which better conduct can grow. For example, someone who admits a failure has already taken the first step toward changing it.

298.text: Water cleans the body, but truthfulness cleans the mind. Honest words and actions remove the hidden dirt of guilt and deceit. For example, telling the truth about a mistake brings more real peace than hiding it behind excuses.

299.text: Lights can remove darkness around us, but truth is the light that guides a wise person within. Honesty helps us see our choices clearly. For example, a student who admits cheating can finally face the problem and choose to rebuild trust.

300.text: Among all the qualities we can recognize as great, none is better than truthfulness. It is the virtue that makes other virtues trustworthy. For example, kindness, courage, and generosity mean far more when people can believe the person showing them.

301.text: The real test of self-control is staying calm when you have the power to hurt someone back. Anger that cannot do much damage is easy to hide; anger that can cause harm must be mastered. For example, after a rude message in a group chat, choosing a calm reply shows true strength.

302.text: Anger is harmful when directed at someone stronger, but it is even worse when used against someone who cannot fight back. Power makes angry behavior more dangerous, not more acceptable. For example, a manager should not unload frustration on a new employee just because the employee has less authority.

303.text: Let go of anger toward everyone, because anger becomes the source of many other wrongs. Holding it gives one bad feeling room to create more damage. For example, rereading an angry text before sending it can help you delete the insult instead of starting a larger fight.

304.text: Anger is a powerful enemy because it destroys both the smile on your face and the happiness in your heart. Nothing steals joy faster than carrying anger everywhere. For example, one unresolved argument can spoil an entire day that could have been peaceful.

305.text: If you want to protect yourself, protect yourself from uncontrolled anger. Left unchecked, anger turns against the person who carries it. For example, an angry post made in a moment can damage your friendships, studies, or job long after the feeling has passed.

306.text: Anger is a fire that can destroy not only the angry person but also the friends and family who support them. It burns the very shelter that should keep life steady. For example, one explosive argument can push away people who had stood by you for years.

307.text: Treating anger as a sign of strength only makes you suffer, just as striking the ground hurts the hand that hits it. Anger punishes its owner even when it seems powerful. For example, slamming a desk may frighten others for a moment, but it leaves you hurt, embarrassed, and less trusted.

308.text: Even when someone has hurt you as severely as a fire burns, it is better to let go of anger when peace becomes possible. Forgiveness here means refusing to keep feeding the conflict, not pretending the harm never happened. For example, accepting a sincere apology can stop one painful mistake from destroying an entire relationship.

309.text: A person who does not keep anger in the heart can pursue their good aims with a clear mind. Without anger clouding judgment, progress becomes much more possible. For example, a student who calmly fixes a group-project problem is more likely to finish well than one who spends the time blaming everyone.

310.text: Someone ruled by extreme anger is like a person who has lost the life of good judgment, while someone who gives up anger is like a person brought back to life. Calmness restores the ability to think and care. For example, taking a breath before answering can turn a heated argument into a useful conversation.

311.text: A good person will not hurt others even to gain wealth, status, or a more comfortable life. Success bought with someone else's suffering is not true greatness. For example, taking credit for a coworker's work may bring a promotion, but it damages both fairness and trust.

312.text: A person of character does not return harm for harm, even when someone has deliberately wronged them. Refusing revenge protects your own integrity. For example, answering a hostile classmate with clear boundaries instead of an insult keeps the conflict from spreading.

313.text: Hurting someone who wronged you without cause brings lasting sorrow instead of relief. Revenge adds a new wrong to the original one and can trap you in regret. For example, posting private information about a bully may feel satisfying at first, but it can create consequences you cannot undo.

314.text: The best way to punish someone who harmed you is to answer with such kindness that they feel ashamed of their behavior, then stop keeping score. This does not excuse the wrong; it refuses to become cruel in return. For example, helping a difficult teammate finish fairly can expose the difference between your conduct and theirs.

315.text: Knowledge has little value if it does not help us protect others from pain as carefully as we protect ourselves. Understanding becomes wisdom only when it leads to care. For example, someone who knows how humiliating bullying feels should step in when another person is being targeted.

316.text: Do not do to another person what you already know causes pain from your own experience. Your past suffering can teach you how to treat others better. For example, if being left out once hurt you, make room for the new person instead of repeating it.

317.text: The highest virtue is refusing to knowingly harm anyone, even in a small way, at any time. Good character begins with what we choose not to do. For example, skipping a cruel joke about someone's weakness can protect their dignity.

318.text: If you have felt how painful a wrong can be, why would you deliberately give that same pain to another living being? Personal experience should awaken compassion. For example, after being embarrassed in public, do not pass that humiliation on to a quieter classmate.

319.text: Harm done to others can return to the person who caused it, often when they least expect it. The verse pictures this return as quickly as morning wrongdoing followed by evening trouble. For example, a false rumor may later destroy the trust the rumor-spreader needs from others.

320.text: People who want a life free from harm should not cause harm to anyone else. Pain follows those who make pain their habit. For example, if you want a peaceful online life, do not harass people and then be surprised when conflict comes back to you.

321.text: Not destroying life is presented as the heart of virtuous conduct, because violence opens the way to many other wrongs. Respect for life is a foundation for every other moral choice. For example, choosing dialogue instead of revenge can stop one conflict from becoming a chain of harm.

322.text: The greatest virtue is to share what you have and help many living beings continue safely. Food and resources become truly meaningful when they support more than one person. For example, sharing a meal and helping protect an injured animal both turn what you have into care for life.

323.text: Among moral duties, not destroying life stands first, and honesty follows close behind. A good life needs both compassion and truth. For example, tell the truth about a mistake and solve it without hurting the person who made it.

324.text: The good path is the one that carefully avoids killing or harming any living creature. Moral living requires attention to the life around us, not just good intentions. For example, moving a small creature out of danger instead of crushing it is a simple act of that care.

325.text: Among those who give up worldly attachments, the highest is the person who is especially careful never to destroy life. Renunciation is shown not only by leaving possessions behind but also by protecting living beings. For example, someone who chooses patience over violent revenge demonstrates this deeper discipline.

326.text: The verse honors a person committed to never killing by saying that even death hesitates before such a life. It presents respect for life as a strength that rises above fear. For example, choosing to protect a vulnerable person rather than harm them shows the courage this ideal demands.

327.text: One should not take another person's life even to save one's own. The verse places another life's value above desperate self-interest. For example, refusing to answer danger with deliberate violence can be the hardest and most principled choice a person makes.

328.text: Even a great benefit gained by killing is considered dishonorable by the wise. A result cannot become truly good when it depends on destroying life. For example, a profitable plan that succeeds by treating living beings as disposable is not something to admire.

329.text: The verse says that people who make a practice of killing are judged as base by those who understand the cruelty of that work. It asks us to measure a livelihood by the harm it causes, not only by the money it earns. For example, refusing to praise violence just because it is profitable keeps compassion in view.

330.text: In the verse's ancient moral view, sages connect a life marked by severe illness and degradation with the consequences of killing in an earlier life. The teaching treats cruelty as a serious act whose effects do not simply disappear. For example, it reminds us that no violent choice should be dismissed as harmless or consequence-free.

331.text: It is deep ignorance to treat temporary things as if they will last forever. Wisdom begins by remembering that possessions, status, and life itself can change. For example, someone who knows popularity can fade will not build their whole identity on online attention.

332.text: Wealth gathers like a crowd arriving for a performance, then disappears like that crowd leaving when the show ends. Having money is temporary, so it should not become the center of life. For example, savings can grow over years and vanish quickly through one major expense.

333.text: Wealth does not last, so use it for lasting good while you have it. Money becomes more valuable when it supports something that outlives the money itself. For example, helping someone learn a skill can matter long after the cash has been spent.

334.text: Each day may look ordinary, but time is quietly cutting down our lives like a blade. The wise notice what the passing days are taking. For example, endless postponing can consume the months you meant to spend with family or on a meaningful goal.

335.text: Do good quickly, before illness or death makes speech and action impossible. The chance to help belongs to the time when we are still able to act. For example, call someone who needs support today instead of assuming there will always be another chance.

336.text: This world shows its impermanence by making someone who was alive yesterday absent today. No person can assume that life will remain unchanged. For example, hearing that a familiar neighbor has died can remind us to value people while they are still with us.

337.text: People make countless plans while forgetting that they may not even have another moment. Planning is useful, but ignoring life's uncertainty is foolish. For example, do not keep postponing an apology or a dream as though time were guaranteed.

338.text: The bond between the soul and the body is compared to a bird leaving the nest or egg behind. The body is a temporary home, not something we can keep forever. For example, caring for your health matters, but it is also wise not to treat appearance as your permanent identity.

339.text: The verse compares death to sleep and birth to waking from it, reflecting the classical idea of life continuing through change. It invites us to see death as part of a larger cycle rather than only an ending. For example, remembering this teaching can help someone face change with less fear and more care for how they live now.

340.text: The soul living in a body has no permanent home there; the body is only a temporary shelter. This image encourages humility about a life that can change at any time. For example, enjoy and care for the life you have without acting as if your present situation can never end.

341.text: Whatever attachment a person gives up, that particular attachment can no longer cause the same pain. Letting go removes the grip of the thing we were clinging to. For example, releasing the need for everyone's approval makes criticism much easier to bear.

342.text: If you want freedom from suffering, let go of attachments while you still have the choice to do so. Afterward, life can still hold many simple joys, without the fear of losing everything. For example, choosing to live with fewer possessions can make a move or financial setback far less frightening.

343.text: A person seeking freedom must master the five senses and release the things they constantly demand. Giving up the object of a craving is part of overcoming the craving itself. For example, turning off an endless stream of shopping or social-media alerts can help break its hold on your attention.

344.text: For someone practicing deep detachment, owning nothing is the natural discipline; possessions can awaken new desires and confusion. One attachment can invite many more. For example, buying one item to feel satisfied may quickly turn into chasing the next purchase.

345.text: Someone trying to end the cycle of birth sees even the body as more than they need, so adding further attachments makes no sense. The teaching points toward radical simplicity and release. For example, a person focused on spiritual freedom will not pile up status, possessions, and obligations around an already demanding life.

346.text: The person who cuts away the pride of “I” and “mine” reaches a state described as higher than even the gods can attain. Freedom begins when the self is no longer built around ownership and ego. For example, sharing credit for a team success instead of claiming it all is a small step away from “mine.”

347.text: Sorrows keep holding on to people who refuse to release their desires. When craving loosens its grip, suffering loses much of its grip too. For example, someone who stops measuring their worth by grades or likes is less shaken when those numbers change.

348.text: Those who renounce every attachment are said to reach the highest freedom, while those who cling remain confused and trapped in the cycle of birth. Partial release does not bring the same clarity as wholehearted detachment. For example, wanting a fresh start while protecting every old harmful habit keeps the same problem alive.

349.text: When attachment is truly abandoned, the cycle of further birth is said to end; while it remains, life keeps shifting through unstable joys and sorrows. The teaching places freedom in complete release, not temporary restraint. For example, ignoring one craving for a day is different from no longer being ruled by it.

350.text: To let go of desire, hold to the One who is free from desire. The verse presents devotion to the desireless divine as a support for releasing our own cravings. For example, choosing a life guided by service and spiritual purpose can make status and possessions less controlling.

351.text: Mistaking what is false for what is real clouds judgment and can lead to a troubled life. For example, treating an online rumor as fact can make someone choose badly and hurt others.

352.text: When confusion clears and we see things honestly, life becomes more peaceful and joyful. For example, checking the facts before reacting can replace needless worry with a calmer decision.

353.text: When honest questioning leads to clear understanding, a higher and more hopeful way of living can feel close. For example, researching a difficult choice can replace uncertainty with confidence about the path ahead.

354.text: Knowing many facts through the senses is not enough if we still fail to understand what is true and important. For example, someone may know how a rumor spread but still lack the wisdom to see that sharing it is harmful.

355.text: Wisdom looks past appearances and asks what something really is. For example, a flashy online offer may seem perfect until you check its hidden costs and actual terms.

356.text: The teaching says that those who learn deeply and recognize truth move toward freedom from the cycle of birth. In everyday life, this also points to leaving behind the habits and attachments that keep pulling us back into the same troubles; for example, choosing self-control instead of repeating a harmful pattern.

357.text: A mind that examines what it has learned and firmly understands truth is no longer trapped by fear of repeated birth. For example, someone who understands the roots of an unhealthy habit can stop expecting the same mistake to control them forever.

358.text: True understanding removes the ignorance that keeps suffering and repeated birth going, and it reveals the truth that brings freedom. For example, noticing an unfair assumption can help someone replace it with a wiser and kinder way of seeing people.

359.text: When we understand what gives suffering its support and loosen our attachment to it, those troubles lose their hold. For example, a person who stops depending on constant praise is less shaken when others do not approve.

360.text: Desire, anger, and confusion feed many troubles; when we stop giving them room, those troubles begin to fade. For example, pausing before sending an angry reply can prevent one heated moment from damaging a friendship.

361.text: The verse describes desire as the seed that keeps the cycle of birth going for every living being. For example, an endless craving for status can keep someone chasing the next achievement without ever feeling free or satisfied.

362.text: If we seek the highest freedom, we should seek freedom from desire itself. For example, wanting enough rather than always wanting more can loosen the pressure to keep upgrading everything we own.

363.text: Freedom from harmful craving is a greater wealth than anything money can buy. For example, someone who is not controlled by brands or other people’s approval can feel rich even with a simple life.

364.text: A clean mind is free from greedy craving, and that freedom grows from loving truth. For example, admitting a mistake instead of protecting your image keeps your mind clearer and your relationships more honest.

365.text: True freedom belongs to those who are free from desire, not merely to people who have given up a few possessions. For example, owning little means little if a person is still consumed by envy of what everyone else has.

366.text: We should watch desire carefully because it can deceive us and lead us to ruin. For example, the wish for a promotion can tempt someone to take credit for a colleague’s work.

367.text: When excessive desire is cut away, a person can choose the actions that protect lasting freedom and well-being. For example, refusing a dishonest shortcut can open the way to a career built on trust rather than fear.

368.text: A person without craving avoids the chain of sorrow, while desire makes trouble return again and again. For example, chasing likes online can turn one disappointing post into a constant cycle of comparison and anxiety.

369.text: When destructive craving, the deepest source of sorrow, is removed, steady joy can remain. For example, someone who stops comparing their life with everyone else’s can enjoy ordinary moments without feeling behind.

370.text: Craving is never fully satisfied; letting it go brings a steadier kind of contentment. For example, ending the habit of endless shopping can make room for gratitude and peace with what is already enough.

371.text: The verse links favorable fortune with tireless effort and difficult fortune with laziness, while reminding us that circumstances can affect how we act. For example, a supported student may find it easier to stay motivated, but should still use that opportunity rather than treat it as guaranteed success.

372.text: Changing circumstances can make a person feel either mentally dull or more capable of understanding. For example, a serious setback may overwhelm someone at first, while good guidance and a better opportunity can help the same person learn and grow.

373.text: Even after studying many subtle books, a person’s own capacity and circumstances still shape how much they understand. For example, two students can read the same lesson yet need different amounts of practice and support to grasp it.

374.text: The world contains different kinds of fortune: one may bring wealth, while another brings clear understanding. For example, a successful business owner may still need to learn from a thoughtful adviser before making a wise decision.

375.text: When building wealth, circumstances can turn an apparently good plan into a loss, or an unlikely plan into a success. For example, a careful small business may struggle because of events beyond its control, while an unexpected opportunity helps another one grow.

376.text: What circumstances do not allow us to keep may slip away despite our care, while what truly remains with us may survive even when we neglect it. For example, a job can disappear despite careful planning, while a learned skill can stay useful through many changes.

377.text: Even people who gather great wealth can enjoy only what their circumstances, time, health, and responsibilities allow. For example, a person may have plenty of money but too little time or health to enjoy it freely.

378.text: The verse suggests that even people without possessions may not be free to renounce worldly life, because difficult circumstances still hold them back. For example, someone may long for a quiet spiritual life but remain responsible for caring for family members.

379.text: If we welcome good fortune as part of life’s changes, we should not be destroyed when difficult fortune arrives. For example, a student who celebrates a high score can also face a low one with patience and a plan to improve.

380.text: The verse presents fate as a force that can outlast our attempts to avoid it, encouraging humility about what we cannot control. For example, a carefully planned trip may be changed by a sudden emergency, even though wise preparation still matters.

381.text: A strong ruler needs six supports: capable defenders, loyal people, sufficient resources, wise advisers, dependable allies, and secure protection. For example, a community leader needs a skilled team, public trust, a workable budget, partners, and a plan for emergencies.

382.text: A good leader needs courage, generosity, wisdom, and steady energy. For example, a student team captain must speak up about unfairness, share credit, make thoughtful choices, and keep working when a project becomes difficult.

383.text: Anyone responsible for a country or community should stay alert, keep learning, and act with courage. For example, a manager who notices problems early, studies the facts, and makes a fair decision can protect the whole team.

384.text: The best ruler follows justice, removes wrongdoing, and protects the dignity and courage of the people. For example, a manager should enforce a fair rule even when the person who broke it is a close friend.

385.text: Good government must create resources, collect them, protect them, and use them wisely. For example, a school club can raise money, keep clear records, guard its budget, and spend it on the activities members actually need.

386.text: People respect a leader who is easy to approach and does not use harsh words. For example, employees are more likely to report a problem early when their manager listens calmly instead of attacking the messenger.

387.text: Kind speech, generous help, and protection for those who depend on a leader earn trust and cooperation. For example, a mentor who speaks respectfully and supports a struggling student can inspire that student to help others too.

388.text: A ruler who governs fairly and protects the people earns deep respect, almost like a guardian with sacred authority. For example, a school leader who handles bullying seriously and applies rules equally becomes someone students trust.

389.text: A strong leader can listen patiently even when criticism is painful, especially when it points out a real problem. For example, a team manager who accepts difficult feedback can fix a mistake before it harms everyone.

390.text: A ruler shines when they combine generosity, compassion, justice, and care for the people. For example, a community leader can support families in need, treat opponents fairly, enforce clear rules, and protect the vulnerable.

391.text: Learn what is worth learning thoroughly, then let your actions match that knowledge. For example, someone who studies honesty but still cheats on an assignment has not truly lived by the lesson.

392.text: Reading and working with numbers are like two eyes: both help us understand the world clearly. For example, reading the terms of a loan and calculating its cost can prevent a serious mistake.

393.text: Learning is described as giving people eyes because it helps them notice and understand what is around them. For example, a person who learns to question evidence can see through a misleading advertisement more easily.

394.text: A learned and gracious person makes others happy when they meet and leaves them glad to meet again. For example, a classmate who listens warmly and includes everyone is remembered with affection after the conversation ends.

395.text: People who humbly seek learning rise above those who refuse to learn, just as the needy seek help from the wealthy. For example, asking a teacher to explain a difficult idea shows strength and opens the door to growth.

396.text: Knowledge grows with study just as water rises from a well as it is dug deeper. For example, practicing a language a little every day steadily gives someone more words and confidence.

397.text: Learning helps a person feel at home in every country and town, so there is little reason to stop learning while life continues. For example, knowing other languages and customs can help someone make friends wherever they travel.

398.text: Learning gained in one life is described as a lasting benefit that continues through many births and generations. For example, a useful skill learned today can support a person for years and be passed on to their children.

399.text: People who learn deeply want to keep learning when they see that their knowledge brings joy and benefit to others as well as to themselves. For example, a programmer may enjoy solving a problem even more after teaching the solution to the whole team.

400.text: Learning is an enduring kind of wealth because it stays useful when possessions and circumstances change. For example, a practical skill can help someone rebuild after losing a job, while money alone may eventually run out.

401.text: Knowledge gives your words a firm foundation; speaking without it is like playing a game without a board. For example, joining a class debate without reading the material leaves you guessing when others ask questions.

402.text: Wanting to speak confidently without first learning is like claiming a skill you have never practised. For example, commenting on a group project without reading the instructions can make your confidence look empty.

403.text: Even someone without formal learning shows good judgment by listening quietly before knowledgeable people. For example, a new volunteer can learn a great deal by watching experienced teammates before offering advice.

404.text: Natural cleverness is valuable, but wise people also look for study, evidence, and practice before calling it knowledge. For example, a quick idea becomes trustworthy only after you test it and learn what the facts show.

405.text: Pretending to know more than you do usually falls apart when real questions begin; honest humility is stronger. For example, someone who bluffs through an interview may be exposed as soon as the interviewer asks for details.

406.text: A person who refuses to learn may be alive, but has little opportunity to contribute; learning makes our abilities useful. For example, someone who ignores every training session cannot reliably help a team when a problem appears.

407.text: Good looks or a polished image mean little without the understanding to support them, like a beautifully painted clay figure. For example, an impressive presentation is empty if its speaker cannot explain the basic facts behind it.

408.text: Wealth in the hands of someone without judgment can cause more harm than poverty borne by a wise person. For example, an inexperienced owner may waste money and hurt workers, while a careful person can use very little well.

409.text: Birth, status, or family name does not create the dignity that learning and character bring. For example, a student from a modest background may earn greater respect through knowledge and fairness than a privileged student who has not prepared.

410.text: Learning helps people reason, understand one another, and choose their actions instead of merely reacting to instinct. For example, studying history can help a young person question a crowd and make a thoughtful choice.

411.text: The wealth gained by listening to wise people is greater than money because it improves every decision that follows. For example, one honest conversation with a mentor may prevent an expensive mistake.

412.text: When there is no chance to feed the mind through good conversation or teaching, even a little food can satisfy the body. For example, during a quiet break, sharing a useful lesson can matter more than simply filling the time with snacks.

413.text: People who nourish themselves through listening and learning gain a dignity that rises above their circumstances. For example, a student who learns from every teacher can grow in wisdom even without wealth or privilege.

414.text: Even without formal education, listening to people who know more can become a steady support in difficult times. For example, an apprentice who follows a mentor's advice can handle a crisis more calmly.

415.text: Advice from a principled and experienced person steadies you when the path feels slippery. For example, a trusted friend can stop you from signing a risky online loan when excitement clouds your judgment.

416.text: Even a small piece of good instruction can add lasting dignity and strength. For example, one helpful suggestion from a teacher may turn an ordinary presentation into a clear and confident one.

417.text: People who study and listen carefully do not speak foolishly, even when they may have misunderstood something; they pause and think. For example, they say they need to check a rumour instead of repeating it as fact.

418.text: Ears that hear sounds but refuse every useful lesson are effectively deaf. For example, someone who ignores a safety briefing may hear every word and still repeat the same avoidable mistake.

419.text: Careful listening teaches humility and respectful speech; without it, confidence can become rudeness. For example, a person who asks questions before interrupting is more likely to speak kindly and wisely.

420.text: A life devoted only to physical pleasures, while ignoring meaningful ideas, misses much of what makes life worthwhile. For example, someone who spends every free moment on food and entertainment may never make time for a conversation that broadens the mind.

421.text: Wisdom protects you like an inner fortress: it can prevent harm and cannot easily be taken away by an opponent. For example, knowing how to check a suspicious message can protect you from an online scam.

422.text: Wisdom does not let the mind follow every impulse; it turns attention away from harm and toward what is good. For example, pausing before sending an angry message can keep a disagreement from becoming a lasting wound.

423.text: Wisdom looks for truth in an idea no matter who says it, instead of trusting popularity or status. For example, you check the evidence before forwarding a rumour shared by a close friend.

424.text: Wisdom explains difficult ideas in simple words and can also notice the deeper meaning in someone else's words. For example, a good team leader makes an assignment clear while listening for a teammate's unspoken concern.

425.text: Wise friendship with good people stays steady instead of blooming with excitement and then fading away. For example, a dependable friend supports you during both exam success and disappointment.

426.text: Wisdom means living in harmony with responsible people and sound ways of life, not blindly following every trend. For example, joining a group that respects safety and fairness is wiser than copying whatever the crowd does.

427.text: Wise people think ahead about likely results; unwise people notice only what feels easy right now. For example, a student who plans for rent and bills will not spend the whole paycheque on a sudden impulse.

428.text: Ignoring a real danger is not courage; wise people take proper fear as a signal to act carefully. For example, wearing a helmet before cycling is sensible, not timid.

429.text: People who foresee trouble and prepare for it are less likely to be overwhelmed when it arrives. For example, keeping a backup of important files can prevent a broken laptop from becoming a disaster.

430.text: Wisdom can make a person rich in what matters even without many possessions, while possessions are empty without good judgment. For example, someone with a small budget can build a secure life by planning, while careless wealth can disappear quickly.

431.text: A leader becomes truly great by keeping pride, anger, and degrading desires under control. For example, a manager who accepts criticism calmly earns more respect than one who uses power to intimidate people.

432.text: A leader is weakened by hoarding what others need, clinging to empty pride, or enjoying harmful pleasures. For example, a club leader who keeps all the funds, rejects good advice, and humiliates volunteers damages the whole group.

433.text: People who care about their good name treat even a tiny wrong as something serious. For example, they correct a copied sentence in an assignment instead of telling themselves that a small piece of cheating does not matter.

434.text: A person's own faults are a more dangerous enemy than any outside rival, so protecting character must come first. For example, stopping a small lie before it grows into a cover-up can save a whole team's trust.

435.text: A life can collapse quickly when warning signs are ignored instead of being dealt with early. For example, refusing to repair a small leak may leave a home badly damaged after the next storm.

436.text: Before judging other people's faults, a leader should remove the same faults from their own conduct. For example, a team captain should admit being late before demanding better punctuality from everyone else.

437.text: Wealth that is hoarded instead of being used for its rightful purposes eventually becomes useless or disappears. For example, an organisation that saves every coin but never maintains its equipment may lose the very resources it meant to protect.

438.text: Extreme stinginess is more than an ordinary fault because it prevents wealth from doing any good. For example, someone who refuses every necessary repair may eventually lose far more than the cost of fixing the problem.

439.text: Do not become dazzled by your own importance, and do not chase actions that bring no real benefit. For example, a team leader can skip a flashy project for likes and choose work that genuinely helps people.

440.text: Keep important plans private until they are ready, because careless disclosure can give opponents a chance to interfere. For example, a small business may protect a new product idea until it is prepared to launch it.

441.text: Choose the friendship of ethical, experienced people after considering their character and the value of their guidance. For example, a young worker who seeks a thoughtful mentor can avoid mistakes that enthusiasm alone would cause.

442.text: Keep close to people who can solve present problems and prevent the same problems from returning. For example, an experienced teammate can fix a failing project and help the group build a better process for next time.

443.text: One of the rarest achievements is earning the trust of truly great people and making them close allies. For example, a respected coach is more likely to mentor a young player who consistently shows honesty and effort.

444.text: One of the greatest strengths is to work with people who know more than you and follow sound guidance. For example, a junior developer who welcomes a senior colleague's review grows faster and avoids costly errors.

445.text: A leader should choose advisers as carefully as eyes, checking both their ability and their character. For example, a student-group president should choose a treasurer for honesty and skill, not just friendship.

446.text: People who surround themselves with capable and ethical allies leave enemies little room to harm them. For example, a small business with reliable partners can withstand pressure that would overwhelm its owner alone.

447.text: A leader who keeps advisers willing to give firm, honest correction is difficult to ruin. For example, a board member who warns about an unsafe decision may save an entire organisation from a costly mistake.

448.text: Without people who can point out mistakes, even an unopposed leader can destroy their own work. For example, a group leader who listens only to praise may miss a budget problem until the project fails.

449.text: Effort cannot last without dependable support, just as a business cannot earn without some capital to begin with. For example, a community project needs committed people and basic resources if it is to continue after its first success.

450.text: Losing the friendship of good and wise people is worse than making many enemies because their guidance and support are hard to replace. For example, leaving a trusted team just to chase popularity can cost you the people who helped you grow.

451.text: The people around you can reveal and shape your character. For example, choosing honest friends makes it easier to resist cheating and harmful habits.

452.text: Your surroundings influence how you think and behave, just as soil changes the water that flows through it. For example, a student in a focused study group may build better habits.

453.text: Your mind gives you the ability to understand, but your companions strongly affect how others judge your character. For example, a responsible person may still be mistrusted if they constantly join reckless friends.

454.text: Wisdom may seem to come from within, but good companions help it grow and become useful. For example, a mentor can help you notice a better answer than you would find alone.

455.text: Clean company supports clean thoughts and clean actions. For example, friends who refuse to copy homework make it easier for everyone to act honestly.

456.text: A pure mind can leave a good legacy, and good companions make good actions easier to carry out. For example, a caring volunteer can do even more when surrounded by dependable helpers.

457.text: A healthy mind supports a good life, while a good community brings lasting respect. For example, reliable friends can help you recover from a setback and earn others’ trust.

458.text: Even a good person needs good company to protect and strengthen their character. For example, honest friends can stop you from making a choice you would later regret.

459.text: Inner goodness brings lasting value, and the company of good people strengthens it. For example, a service group can help someone keep living by their values when life becomes difficult.

460.text: Good companions are one of life’s greatest supports, while harmful companions can bring deep trouble. For example, the right friends encourage growth instead of pulling you into risky behavior.

461.text: Before acting, consider what you may lose, what you may gain, and what the final result could be. For example, compare the cost, risks, and long-term value before accepting a new job.

462.text: Think carefully with trusted, capable people before starting, and difficult goals become more manageable. For example, a project team that plans together can solve problems no member could handle alone.

463.text: Do not risk what you already have for a profit that is only a hope. For example, putting all your savings into a tempting scheme could leave you with neither the investment nor the promised gain.

464.text: Do not begin a plan that has not been tested and understood, especially if failure would bring shame. For example, check the facts before presenting an unverified claim to your whole class.

465.text: Starting without studying every part of a plan can make the opposition stronger. For example, entering a competition without preparing may give a rival an easy advantage.

466.text: Doing what is wrong can cause harm, but failing to do what is right can also cause harm. For example, cheating is wrong, yet refusing to study or help when you should can also lead to failure.

467.text: Think through an action before you begin; deciding to think about it only afterward is careless. For example, plan the steps and deadline of a group project before promising to finish it.

468.text: Even strong support cannot save work done by the wrong method. For example, a large group may still fail a project if no one agrees on how the work should be done.

469.text: Even a good action can go wrong when it ignores a person’s nature and situation. For example, advice that motivates one friend may embarrass another, so help should be offered with understanding.

470.text: Choose actions that fit your role and will not bring justified disrespect. For example, a team leader should keep promises instead of making flashy claims they cannot fulfill.

471.text: Before acting, weigh the task, your own strength, the other side’s strength, and the support available to both. For example, a small team should check its skills and resources before taking on a major competitor.

472.text: Know what you can do, learn what the task requires, and stay focused on it. For example, someone who studies the tools needed for a difficult skill can achieve more than someone who relies only on enthusiasm.

473.text: Many people start boldly without knowing their limits and fail before they finish. For example, taking on five demanding commitments at once can leave every one of them incomplete.

474.text: A person who ignores others, misunderstands their own limits, and admires their own greatness can fall quickly. For example, a boastful team leader may lose everyone’s cooperation and fail the project.

475.text: Even small burdens become dangerous when too many are piled together. For example, a backpack that feels light at first can tear or hurt your back when it is overloaded.

476.text: Once you have reached your safe limit, pushing farther can turn success into danger. For example, continuing up a difficult trail after ignoring warning signs can put your life at risk.

477.text: Give according to what you can truly afford; measured generosity protects your ability to keep helping. For example, set a donation budget instead of promising money you cannot spare.

478.text: A modest income is not harmful when spending stays within it. For example, a student can manage a small allowance well by avoiding debt and unnecessary purchases.

479.text: A life lived beyond its means may look prosperous for a while, but it cannot last. For example, constant credit-card spending can make success disappear under growing bills.

480.text: Generosity without regard for your resources can quickly destroy what you have. For example, repeatedly paying every friend’s expenses may leave you unable to meet your own needs.

481.text: Even the weaker side can succeed when it chooses the right time to act. For example, presenting a proposal when decision-makers are ready to listen is wiser than forcing it at a busy moment.

482.text: Acting in season and at the right moment helps success stay secure. For example, applying for a course before its deadline keeps an opportunity from slipping away.

483.text: With the right tools and the right timing, few tasks are truly impossible. For example, a student with good resources and a well-chosen study schedule can master a difficult subject.

484.text: The right time and place can make even a very ambitious goal possible. For example, presenting a strong idea to the people who can support it gives the idea a real chance to succeed.

485.text: People who aim high do not panic; they prepare and wait for the right moment. For example, an athlete may train patiently instead of competing before being ready.

486.text: Holding back can be preparation, not fear. For example, a runner may wait for the right opening before making the final move in a race.

487.text: Wise people do not display anger at once; they stay calm and choose a useful moment to respond. For example, pausing before replying to an insulting message can prevent a needless argument.

488.text: When faced with an opponent, patience and courtesy can be wiser than a rushed reaction. For example, calmly keeping records during a dispute may let the truth become clear when the other person makes a mistake.

489.text: When a rare opportunity appears, act while it is available. For example, apply for a scholarship before its short deadline instead of waiting for a better chance that may never come.

490.text: Wait quietly when the time is not right, then act accurately when it is. For example, a careful applicant can prepare in silence and submit a strong application when the opening appears.

491.text: Do not begin until you have chosen the right setting, and do not underestimate the challenge. For example, learn the rules and choose a suitable venue before starting a difficult debate.

492.text: Even strong people gain many advantages from a secure base. For example, a team with reliable equipment, clear support, and a safe place to work can handle pressure better.

493.text: A weaker side can succeed by choosing favorable conditions and protecting itself. For example, a small business may compete successfully by serving one local need better than a much larger company.

494.text: Choosing the right ground and staying committed can overturn a stronger opponent’s plan. For example, a small team with a clear specialty can make a larger competitor abandon an easy victory.

495.text: Strength depends on the environment where it is used. For example, an excellent swimmer may struggle on a steep mountain, while a climber is strongest on the ground they know.

496.text: Every tool has a setting where it works best. For example, a bicycle is useful on a road but cannot replace a boat on open water.

497.text: Careful planning and a suitable setting can leave courage as the main support you need. For example, a well-prepared speaker can face a large audience without depending on constant help.

498.text: A large force can lose its advantage in a place that favors only a small force. For example, a huge team may struggle in a narrow project while a focused pair works efficiently.

499.text: Even people without great defenses are difficult to defeat on their own ground. For example, a visiting team may face a strong challenge because the local team knows the field and conditions better.

500.text: Great strength can fail when it is trapped in the wrong conditions. For example, an expert who ignores an unfamiliar system may be outperformed by a less powerful person who understands that setting.

501.text: Choose a leader after seeing how they handle honesty, money, temptation, and danger. For example, before making someone a team captain, notice whether they stay fair when they could profit or escape blame.

502.text: Trust someone who has a good reputation, avoids wrongdoing, and feels ashamed to harm others. For example, choose a club treasurer who is careful with shared money and admits mistakes.

503.text: Even a highly educated person can still have blind spots. For example, a top student should still ask questions and accept feedback before leading a difficult project.

504.text: Judge a person by both their strengths and their faults, then see which side is stronger. For example, when choosing a project partner, look beyond charm and notice whether their reliable habits outweigh their careless ones.

505.text: A person’s actions reveal their real character more clearly than their image or words. For example, someone who quietly helps a teammate under pressure shows more than someone who only talks about being kind.

506.text: Be careful about giving power to someone who feels no responsibility to others or to their own reputation. For example, a group should not hand its shared funds to a person who thinks no one can hold them accountable.

507.text: Do not give an important role to someone who lacks the needed understanding just because you care about them. For example, choose the friend who knows how to manage the event, not the friend you feel closest to.

508.text: Choosing someone without checking their character can create trouble for many people, even in the future. For example, hiring a person without checking their record can leave an entire team dealing with the damage.

509.text: Do not trust people without examining them first; once you have examined someone carefully, trust them in the role that fits them. For example, after checking a volunteer’s skills, let them lead the part of the event they can handle best.

510.text: Choosing someone without checking them and then doubting someone you have checked both cause lasting trouble. For example, a manager who hires carelessly and second-guesses every capable worker will damage the whole team.

511.text: Weigh both the good and the harm in a choice, then choose the person who naturally works toward what is good. For example, select a teammate who considers the risks but still looks for the fairest solution.

512.text: A capable worker grows resources, creates value, and looks ahead for problems that could waste them. For example, a small-business manager should find new customers, use profits wisely, and fix supply issues before they become crises.

513.text: A trustworthy worker combines care for others, good judgment, clear thinking, and freedom from greed. For example, a team leader should support the group, understand the task, decide calmly, and not use the budget for personal gain.

514.text: People may act differently when the kind of work changes, even after careful testing. For example, a student who excels at planning may struggle when asked to speak in front of a crowd.

515.text: Give important work to someone who understands it and can persist through obstacles, not simply to a friend or favorite. For example, choose the experienced organizer for the fundraiser even if your closest friend wants the role.

516.text: Before acting, consider who will do the work, what the work requires, and when the time is right. For example, plan a school event around the team’s skills, the task’s difficulty, and the date’s practical limits.

517.text: Entrust a task only after deciding that a particular person can complete it with the available tools and support. For example, give the video edit to the teammate with the right software and enough time to finish it.

518.text: Once you know what work someone is suited for, place them in that kind of work. For example, let the person who enjoys careful checking handle the team’s final proofreading.

519.text: Do not treat a hardworking person’s loyalty as suspicious without good reason; mistrust can drive away success. For example, a manager who listens to rumors about a reliable employee may lose the very person keeping the project on track.

520.text: A leader should regularly check that the people doing the work remain honest and steady, because their conduct shapes everyone else. For example, a manager who reviews safety practices each day helps the whole workplace take them seriously.

521.text: True relatives and close friends keep showing care even when someone has lost money or status. For example, a family may welcome a relative home after a failed business instead of valuing them only for what they owned.

522.text: A family or circle of friends that keeps its affection through hard times gives lasting strength and support. For example, relatives who encourage someone after a job loss can help them recover and begin again.

523.text: Wealth has little value when a person never shares life with the people who care about them. For example, a successful young professional who shuts everyone out may have comfort but still feel deeply alone.

524.text: One benefit of having wealth is being able to live with and support the people close to you. For example, someone who earns well can make time for family and help them through a difficult season.

525.text: Generosity and warm speech draw people into lasting relationships. For example, a student who shares useful notes and speaks kindly will usually find classmates ready to help in return.

526.text: Generosity and a calm temper make a person welcome to many others. For example, a teammate who shares credit and does not explode over small mistakes becomes someone people want beside them.

527.text: Like a crow calling others to share its food, people should not hide every good thing for themselves. For example, a colleague who shares an opportunity with the team helps everyone grow instead of keeping all the advantage.

528.text: Fair leadership does not mean treating every person identically; it means recognizing each person’s merit and giving suitable support. For example, a coach may assign different roles according to each player’s strengths while respecting the whole team.

529.text: People who left after a conflict may return when the reason for the conflict is gone, especially if you were not the cause. For example, a friend who stepped away during a misunderstanding may reconnect after the truth becomes clear.

530.text: When someone who left returns, listen carefully to why they came back before restoring the relationship. For example, welcome a former teammate who wants to rejoin, but first understand what changed and what support they need.

531.text: Being carried away by happiness can make you forget duties, and that carelessness may cause more harm than a burst of anger. For example, after celebrating a win, a team might miss an important deadline because no one checked the schedule.
