532.text: Repeated forgetfulness can destroy a good reputation just as constant hardship can weaken a person’s learning. For example, someone who keeps forgetting promises will eventually lose friends’ trust, even if they mean well.

533.text: A person who is careless and forgetful cannot build lasting respect. For example, a student who never prepares, misses commitments, and ignores details will not be trusted with an important role.

534.text: Good opportunities and strong protection are useless if carelessness makes you fail to use them. For example, owning an excellent laptop does not help a student who repeatedly forgets to save their work.

535.text: If you fail to prepare for trouble, you may only regret that mistake after the damage is done. For example, someone who never backs up important files may mourn the loss after a device breaks.

536.text: Being attentive and dependable toward everyone, at all times, is one of the greatest strengths a person can have. For example, a nurse who carefully remembers each patient’s needs earns trust through steady attention.

537.text: With careful attention and steady effort, very few worthwhile tasks are beyond reach. For example, a learner can master a difficult skill by remembering each step and practicing it regularly.

538.text: Respect the good practices praised by wise people and make them part of your life; simply admiring them is not enough. For example, a student who praises honesty but cheats when work is hard gains no lasting benefit.

539.text: When success makes you feel excited and secure, remember people who fell because they became careless. For example, after winning a competition, a team should still review its mistakes instead of assuming it cannot fail.

540.text: Keeping a worthy goal in mind makes it easier to reach it. For example, a student who remembers the plan to pass an exam is more likely to study a little each day instead of giving up.

541.text: Justice means examining the facts, avoiding favoritism, and responding in a balanced way. For example, a teacher should hear both students in a dispute before deciding what consequence is fair.

542.text: People thrive under fair and responsible leadership, just as living things depend on rain. For example, students work and learn better when their school has clear rules that apply equally to everyone.

543.text: A just government gives learning, good conduct, and shared values a stable foundation. For example, a community library and school can flourish when leaders protect them fairly and consistently.

544.text: People stand behind a leader who protects them, treats them with care, and governs fairly. For example, residents are more willing to support a local leader who listens to their concerns and acts for the whole neighborhood.

545.text: The poem links just rule with a country’s prosperity, like rain arriving in season and crops growing well. For example, fair and reliable rules help farmers plan their work and give communities a better chance to thrive.

546.text: Lasting success comes more from fair leadership than from force or impressive weapons. For example, a team follows a leader who keeps promises and makes fair decisions more willingly than one who only gives orders.

547.text: A ruler protects people, but justice also protects the ruler from losing their trust. For example, a club leader who applies the same rules to friends and strangers is less likely to face conflict or rebellion.

548.text: A leader who is hard to reach and refuses to examine complaints will eventually lose respect and authority. For example, a manager who ignores repeated reports of unfair treatment may drive away good workers and damage the organization.

549.text: Protecting people and correcting serious wrongdoing are duties of leadership, not signs of weakness. For example, a school must stop bullying and apply a fair consequence even when the student responsible is popular.

550.text: The poem uses a strong image: a ruler must remove murderous criminals to protect innocent people, just as a farmer removes weeds to save crops. For example, a court may lawfully keep a violent offender from harming others after a fair trial.

551.text: A leader who uses public power to oppress people can be more harmful than a single criminal because their decisions affect an entire community. Authority carries a duty to protect, not exploit. For example, a corrupt official who takes money from vulnerable families and denies them basic services causes widespread harm through the power entrusted to them.

552.text: When a ruler demands money through fear rather than fair law, it is little different from a robber holding a weapon. A club leader who threatens members into paying for personal expenses is abusing authority, not collecting a fair contribution.

553.text: A government must keep examining wrongs and correcting them; if it stops, the country slowly falls apart. In a student council, ignoring repeated bullying complaints can quickly make the whole school feel unsafe.

554.text: A ruler who acts without thinking and twists justice can lose both the nation's resources and its people's trust. A business owner who keeps cheating workers may soon lose skilled staff and customers.

555.text: The suffering and tears of abused people can eventually destroy an oppressor's wealth and power. A company that underpays and humiliates staff may face resignations, boycotts, and collapse.

556.text: A ruler's reputation lasts when it is built on fair government; power without justice is quickly forgotten. A team captain is remembered for consistent fairness, not for having the loudest voice.

557.text: Just as land cannot live without rain, people cannot thrive under a ruler without compassion. A principal who listens and helps students in difficulty can make a whole school feel secure.

558.text: Wealth brings little comfort when an unjust ruler can seize or misuse it; living safely matters more than owning much. A shop owner may envy no one if authorities can demand bribes at any time.

559.text: The verse links a ruler's justice with the land's prosperity, warning that bad rule disrupts the conditions that sustain life. When officials neglect irrigation and farmers, even a rainy season can fail to feed the community.

560.text: When those responsible for protecting a society fail, farming, useful work, and learning all suffer. If a town leaves its water system unsafe, farms lose crops and schools lose the stability needed to teach.

561.text: A just ruler examines a wrong carefully and gives a proportionate consequence that prevents it from happening again. If a student damages shared equipment, hearing both sides and requiring fair repair teaches responsibility better than public humiliation.

562.text: Strong leadership can begin an investigation firmly but should not punish more harshly than the facts require. A coach may take a safety violation seriously, then choose a measured consequence that helps a player improve.

563.text: A ruler who governs by making people afraid is already heading toward ruin. A manager who shouts and threatens may get silence for a while, but talented workers soon leave.

564.text: When people regularly describe their ruler as cruel, that ruler's power and honor will not last. An online community led by someone known for harshness will quickly lose members and respect.

565.text: Wealth owned by someone who is impossible to approach and always cold becomes frightening rather than admirable. A rich employer who never meets workers and treats every request with contempt may have money but no goodwill.

566.text: Money cannot remain secure under a leader who speaks harshly and shows no compassion. A successful founder who insults staff may soon lose the people whose work created that success.

567.text: Cruel words and excessive punishment wear down a ruler's strength, just as a file wears down metal. A school that suspends students for every small mistake will lose trust and cooperation.

568.text: A leader who leaves decisions entirely to advisers and then blames them in anger weakens their own position. A project lead who never checks the plan but explodes at the team after failure will lose both respect and results.

569.text: A ruler who makes no preparation before danger arrives will panic and fall when the crisis comes. A family that waits until a storm to discover it has no emergency supplies is learning the same lesson.

570.text: Tyranny is made worse when a cruel ruler gathers unwise people to carry out harmful orders; such a system becomes a burden to everyone. A corrupt club leader may surround themselves with friends who never question unfair decisions.

571.text: The world is held together by the rare beauty of a kind and gracious manner. A calm greeting from a teacher can help a nervous student feel able to ask for help.

572.text: Everyday life works because people show one another consideration; without it, even living together becomes a burden. Letting an exhausted passenger sit down is a small act that keeps a shared space humane.

573.text: Eyes are not truly useful if they see people but show no compassion, just as music fails without harmony. Noticing a classmate being left out and choosing to include them gives sight a human purpose.

574.text: Eyes that never lead to care may be present in the face but do little good. A friend who watches someone struggle and refuses even a simple check-in is seeing without concern.

575.text: Kindness is what makes a person's eyes beautiful; without it, they are only eyes, not a source of comfort. A friendly look from a cashier can ease a customer's bad day.

576.text: People who have eyes but never look on others with compassion are like trees: alive in form but not responsive in spirit. A student who notices a classmate crying yet walks past has missed the human duty of care.

577.text: A person who never shows compassion is described as having no true sight; real seeing includes noticing others' needs. A teammate who spots someone struggling and offers help is using their eyes wisely.

578.text: The highest leadership balances compassion with responsibility, so mercy does not damage the work that must be done. A teacher can give a student another chance while still keeping the class's safety rules.

579.text: The highest patience is to show kindness even to someone who has hurt you, without abandoning justice. Answering a rude message calmly instead of escalating can stop a conflict from spreading.

580.text: True civility can keep us from answering betrayal with hatred, though it does not require staying in danger. If a friend breaks your trust, you can set a boundary and still speak without revenge.

581.text: A ruler needs trustworthy information and sound law as two eyes. A student council making a budget should hear accurate reports and follow its written rules.

582.text: A ruler must stay informed about what is happening among all groups, not just hear flattering reports. A mayor who checks conditions in every neighborhood can respond before a small problem becomes a crisis.

583.text: Gathering reports is not enough; a ruler must understand what they mean and act on the lessons. A team leader who collects feedback but never notices the recurring problem will not improve the project.

584.text: A trustworthy investigator examines allies, relatives, employees, and opponents without favoritism. When a school reviews a complaint, it should hear from friends and critics alike instead of trusting only its own circle.

585.text: A skilled spy can move without arousing suspicion, remain calm under scrutiny, and keep the mission private. In ordinary life, a journalist investigating corruption must protect sources and not reveal the work before it is verified.

586.text: The best spy can enter difficult places in disguise, learn what is needed, and keep their identity secret despite pressure. An undercover investigator may face intense questioning yet protect the investigation until the facts are safe.

587.text: Good investigation uncovers what is hidden and separates solid facts from doubt. Before sharing a serious accusation online, check the original evidence and confirm what actually happened.

588.text: Important information should be checked independently before a ruler acts on it. Before reposting a shocking claim, compare it with a reliable second source.

589.text: Reports are more trustworthy when independent investigators reach the same conclusion; they should not simply copy one another. A school investigating missing funds might ask three people separately and compare their accounts.

590.text: A ruler must reward a spy discreetly, because public praise can expose both the spy and the secret. A student who quietly reports a safety risk should be thanked privately, not identified in front of everyone.

591.text: A person's drive is a deeper form of wealth than possessions; without it, other advantages may go unused. A student with little equipment but steady effort can accomplish more than someone with every resource and no motivation.

592.text: Inner strength is lasting wealth; money and possessions can disappear. A young worker who develops skills and resilience can rebuild after losing a job.

593.text: Someone with lasting determination does not believe life is over when money is lost, because they still possess the will to begin again. After a failed small business, an owner who learns from it and starts carefully shows this strength.

594.text: Steady effort creates opportunities, and success is more likely to reach those who keep working with purpose. A learner who practices a skill every week is more likely to find work using it.

595.text: A person's growth is often as large as the vision and effort they carry within. Someone who begins coding with a serious goal and keeps learning can rise far beyond their first small project.

596.text: Let your aims be worthy and high; even when circumstances stop you, noble ambition still shapes your character and direction. A student who aims to build a useful invention may not finish it, but the goal can guide years of learning.

597.text: People with courage do not give up when setbacks wound them, just as an elephant stands firm under arrows. After failing an exam, a student who reviews mistakes and tries again shows this resilience.

598.text: Without inner strength, a person cannot feel the confidence and joy of giving generously. Someone who has little money but shares time to tutor a neighbor can experience the pride of helping others.

599.text: Physical size and outward power do not guarantee courage; focused determination can overcome them. A smaller player who stays calm and plays bravely may outmatch a stronger opponent.

600.text: What makes a person fully human is the strength to think, choose, and act with purpose; without it, a life can become merely passive. Someone who simply follows every crowd may look independent but is not using their own judgment.

601.text: Idleness can dim even a family's good name, like dust covering a lamp. For example, a student who keeps avoiding responsibilities may eventually damage the reputation their family worked to build.

602.text: Anyone who wants their family to flourish must reject laziness and keep working with purpose. For example, a young person who consistently studies and helps at home strengthens the whole household.

603.text: A foolish person who lives lazily can see their family's good name fade before their own life changes. For example, repeatedly neglecting work or school can bring shame to everyone who supports them.

604.text: When people give in to laziness and make no worthwhile effort, their family's standing falls and their faults multiply. For example, someone who keeps avoiding duties may create more mistakes, conflicts, and financial trouble at home.

605.text: Procrastination, forgetfulness, laziness, and too much sleep together carry a person toward ruin. For example, a student who keeps putting off assignments, forgetting deadlines, and sleeping through study time may soon be overwhelmed.

606.text: Even great wealth or powerful connections cannot help an idle person gain lasting benefit from them. For example, having expensive equipment and expert help means little if someone never makes the effort to use those advantages.

607.text: People who choose laziness instead of serious effort eventually have to hear criticism and ridicule. For example, a teammate who repeatedly fails to do their share will lose the respect of the group.

608.text: If laziness settles into a respected family, it can make its members dependent on those who oppose them. For example, a person who refuses to work may eventually have to accept unfair conditions from someone who controls their livelihood.

609.text: When a person removes laziness, the faults that have harmed their own standing and their family's name can disappear. For example, returning to steady work and keeping promises can slowly restore trust.

610.text: A ruler who never gives in to laziness can fully secure and develop all the land under their care. For example, a leader who acts promptly on public needs can bring the benefits of good planning to an entire community.

611.text: Do not give up by saying that a task is too difficult; steady effort creates the strength to complete it. For example, a student who keeps practicing a hard subject may eventually solve problems that once seemed impossible.

612.text: Do not abandon a task halfway through, because the world loses trust in people who leave their work unfinished. For example, a group project succeeds only when someone follows the plan through to the final detail.

613.text: The ability to support and give generously grows from persistent effort. For example, a person who works steadily can share time, money, or skills when friends or neighbors genuinely need help.

614.text: Promises to help are useless without the effort needed to carry them out, like a powerless person waving a sword. For example, offering to organize an event means little if you will not do the planning and follow-through.

615.text: A person who puts duty before personal comfort can become a strong support for family and friends. For example, someone who finishes important work and still makes time to care for an unwell relative becomes a dependable source of strength.

616.text: Effort can create prosperity, while refusing to work can lead a person into poverty. For example, regularly learning a useful skill can open work opportunities that pass by someone who never tries.

617.text: Laziness invites hardship, while steady effort opens the way to prosperity. For example, a young worker who keeps building skills and showing up reliably is more likely to find good opportunities.

618.text: Lacking good fortune or natural ability is not a disgrace; refusing to learn and act on what you know is. For example, a student may struggle with a subject, but failing to prepare or seek help is the greater fault.

619.text: Even when circumstances prevent the result you hoped for, sincere effort still gives a reward for the work you put in. For example, a rejected job application can still lead to stronger skills and a better next attempt.

620.text: People who keep working without losing heart can eventually overcome obstacles that once seemed fixed by fate. For example, repeated practice can help an athlete or learner break through a limit that earlier failures made seem permanent.

621.text: When trouble arrives, meet it with calm courage instead of panic; that attitude helps drive the trouble away. For example, a student who stays steady after a presentation goes wrong can recover and finish well.

622.text: Even a flood of problems can begin to recede when a wise person calmly looks for a way through them. For example, breaking a huge deadline into smaller steps can make an overwhelming assignment manageable.

623.text: People who do not collapse under hardship make hardship weaker. For example, someone who responds to a setback by finding the next practical step prevents one failure from controlling the rest of their life.

624.text: Persistent effort can wear down trouble, just as a strong ox keeps pulling a cart through deep mud. For example, patiently repairing a difficult project can finally move it past obstacles that stopped quick attempts.

625.text: Even when troubles arrive one after another, a person who does not abandon their purpose can outlast them. For example, someone who keeps studying through several disappointments may eventually pass the exam they once failed.

626.text: People who do not cling selfishly to wealth when they have it need not despair when it is gone. For example, someone who uses prosperity wisely and shares it with others can face a leaner time without feeling that life has lost its worth.

627.text: Wise people know that the body is naturally exposed to pain, so they do not let every discomfort shake their minds. For example, a patient facing a long recovery can accept the difficulty while calmly following the treatment plan.

628.text: A person who does not chase constant pleasure and accepts that hardship is part of life is less likely to be defeated by it. For example, someone who expects training to be uncomfortable is more likely to keep going when progress feels slow.

629.text: Those who do not become overly attached to pleasure are less overwhelmed when pain arrives. For example, a person who enjoys success without depending on it can handle a disappointment without losing balance.

630.text: Someone who can treat hardship as part of the work earns a greatness that even opponents may respect. For example, an athlete who accepts exhausting practice instead of complaining may win the admiration of a rival.

631.text: A capable minister chooses the right tools, timing, method, and plan even for a difficult task. For example, a project leader checks the budget, deadline, people, and process before starting a complex community program.

632.text: A good minister combines courage, protection of the people, learning, sound understanding, and persistent effort. For example, a student leader should stand firm, listen carefully, learn the facts, support the group, and keep working when plans become difficult.

633.text: A capable minister can weaken harmful alliances, protect loyal supporters, and bring back those who have left. For example, a team leader may resolve a conflict, care for current members, and welcome back a former member who has changed.

634.text: A good minister studies what should be done, chooses the best way to do it, and speaks clearly once the decision is made. For example, a leader should compare options, act at the right time, and explain the final plan without wavering.

635.text: The best adviser understands right conduct, speaks with mature judgment, and knows how to turn advice into action. For example, a trusted mentor can explain what is fair, express it clearly, and suggest practical steps that will work.

636.text: Natural intelligence joined with learning can see through even very subtle schemes. For example, an experienced investigator who also studies carefully can notice the hidden flaw in a complicated plan.

637.text: Knowing the theory of an action is not enough; you must understand real people and circumstances and act accordingly. For example, a well-designed app will fail if its creator ignores how the community will actually use it.

638.text: Even if a ruler is ignorant or refuses to listen, a minister must still offer firm and beneficial advice. For example, a team member should respectfully warn a leader about a serious risk instead of staying silent to avoid discomfort.

639.text: A minister who plans harmful or foolish actions can be more dangerous than countless open enemies. For example, a trusted adviser who secretly puts personal gain first can damage an organization from within.

640.text: People without the ability to execute will leave even well-designed plans incomplete. For example, a carefully planned event still fails if no one assigns tasks, solves problems, and finishes the work.

641.text: Skillful speech is a special kind of wealth because it can open understanding and cooperation. For example, a young person who explains an idea clearly may gain support that knowledge alone would not bring.

642.text: Words can bring success or harm, so choose them with care. For example, a thoughtful message can solve a disagreement, while a careless one can damage a friendship or opportunity.

643.text: Good speech holds the attention of those listening and makes even uninterested people want to hear. For example, a presenter who explains an issue clearly and respectfully can engage both supporters and skeptics.

644.text: Understand who is listening and speak in a way they can receive; this is both wise and useful. For example, explain a difficult idea differently to a young child, a classmate, or an expert instead of using the same words for everyone.

645.text: Say something only after testing whether your words are sound and can withstand a better reply. For example, before making a strong claim in a debate, check the evidence and think through the strongest objection.

646.text: Speak so people want to keep listening, and when others speak, look for the useful meaning rather than clinging to their flaws. For example, in a group discussion, present your idea warmly and still learn from a rough but valuable suggestion.

647.text: A person who speaks well, does not tire, and is not intimidated is very hard to defeat in an argument. For example, a calm advocate who knows the facts can continue defending a fair cause even when the room is hostile.

648.text: When people explain ideas clearly, pleasantly, and in the right order, others are ready to act on them. For example, a well-organized set of instructions can help a volunteer team begin work without confusion.

649.text: People who cannot express a clear idea in a few accurate words often hide that weakness by talking too much. For example, a speaker who has not decided what they mean may repeat long explanations instead of giving a direct answer.

650.text: People who cannot explain what they have learned so that others understand are like flowers that bloom without fragrance. For example, knowing a lesson is not enough if you cannot teach its main point clearly to a classmate.

651.text: Good partners can increase your strength, but good work is what brings lasting benefits and fulfills your aims. A supportive team may help you start a project, but careful, honest work is what makes it succeed.

652.text: Avoid actions that bring neither a good reputation nor lasting benefit. Before joining a scheme, ask whether it helps anyone or leaves you ashamed later.

653.text: If you want to grow in respect, avoid choices that damage your good name. A student who refuses to cheat protects the trust they are building.

654.text: Clear-minded people do not choose disgraceful acts even in hardship. When money is tight, someone may still refuse to lie or exploit others for quick relief.

655.text: Do not choose actions you will later regret; if you make such a mistake, learn from it and do not repeat it. After sending a hurtful message, apologize and change how you speak.

656.text: Even urgent need does not justify an act honorable people condemn. Someone struggling to feed family should seek honest help rather than steal from another vulnerable person.

657.text: Honest poverty is better than wealth gained by wrongdoing. A young worker is better off earning modestly than getting rich by scamming customers.

658.text: A forbidden act can still bring suffering even if it succeeds at first. Money gained by cheating may later bring fear, legal trouble, or shame.

659.text: Wealth taken by making others suffer will leave amid suffering, while honestly earned wealth can bear fruit even after a setback. A fair business can recover after a bad season; money taken from workers cannot bring lasting peace.

660.text: Trying to protect wealth gained through deceit is like storing water in an unfired clay pot: it cannot hold. A dishonest deal may look secure, but it can collapse as soon as people uncover it.

661.text: Real strength in completing work comes from strength of mind; other skills matter only when determination guides them. A talented student still needs the discipline to finish the assignment.

662.text: Strong judgment means avoiding destructive choices beforehand and staying steady if trouble still comes. Check a risky plan early, and if it fails anyway, learn and continue without panic.

663.text: Keep important work private until it is finished; announcing it too early can create obstacles. A team should test a project quietly before posting promises it may not keep.

664.text: Anyone can say what they will do; carrying it out as promised is the hard part. It is easy to announce a study plan, but showing up every day proves it.

665.text: People who achieve greatness through firm action earn respect, even from those in power. A reliable organizer gains trust because leaders see that their plans actually work.

666.text: With firm determination, people can achieve what they planned in the way they intended. Someone preparing for an exam reaches the goal by following a steady study plan.

667.text: Do not judge people by size or appearance; a small part can support something great. A quiet student who keeps a team’s project organized may be its most important member.

668.text: Once you have decided clearly, act without hesitation or delay. After choosing to apply for a course, submit the form instead of endlessly putting it off.

669.text: Persist with a worthwhile task even when it is painful at first if it will bring good in the end. Learning a difficult skill may be frustrating now but can open opportunities later.

670.text: The world respects people who are firm in carrying out their work, whatever other abilities they have. A brilliant teammate who never follows through will be trusted less than a dependable one.

671.text: Thoughtful planning should end in a firm decision, and a decision should not be weakened by delay. Once a team has chosen a safe plan, waiting without reason can make the problem worse.

672.text: Some tasks should wait for the right time, but urgent tasks must not be delayed. You can schedule routine studying, but you should act immediately when a friend needs emergency help.

673.text: Finish a task directly when possible; when that route fails, use another suitable way. If an online application fails, submit it through the official alternate channel.

674.text: An unfinished task or unresolved conflict can grow dangerous like a fire left burning. Do not leave a serious misunderstanding or a risky project half dealt with.

675.text: Before acting, consider the resources, tools, timing, method, and place the work requires. Before starting a community event, check the budget, equipment, date, plan, and venue.

676.text: Before starting, consider how the work will end, what obstacles may appear, and what benefit it may bring. Before launching a club, plan its goal, likely problems, and value for members.

677.text: The best way to do a task is to learn from someone who truly understands it. Before repairing a bicycle, ask an experienced mechanic how to do it safely.

678.text: One task can help accomplish another, just as one elephant can help capture another. A research project can also build the skills and contacts needed for a later opportunity.

679.text: Winning over an enemy can be more urgent than doing another favor for a friend. Clearing up a serious dispute with a rival teammate may protect the whole group.

680.text: When weaker leaders face a stronger power, they may accept its terms to protect their people. A small community may cooperate with a larger organization when resistance would put residents at risk.

681.text: A good ambassador needs affection for their people, a respected character, and qualities their ruler can trust. A student representing a club should care about its members and behave in a way that earns confidence.

682.text: A messenger needs loyalty, understanding, and the skill to choose words carefully. When speaking for a team, know its needs and explain them clearly without creating needless conflict.

683.text: A successful envoy must understand politics and be deeply learned in the matters they discuss. Someone negotiating a school partnership should know both the rules and the interests involved.

684.text: A person sent on an important mission should have sound judgment, a pleasing manner, and well-tested learning. A youth leader asked to meet officials should be informed, composed, and respectful.

685.text: A good messenger speaks briefly, leaves out needless harshness, and presents the message in a way that helps others respond well. When asking another club to cooperate, explain the key point politely instead of blaming them.

686.text: A skilled ambassador studies the subject, remains calm under hostile looks, speaks persuasively, and adapts to the moment. In a tense meeting, a prepared representative stays respectful and chooses the right time to make the request.

687.text: The best messenger knows their duty, chooses the right time and place, and thinks carefully before speaking. A student raising a sensitive issue should plan what to say and speak privately when the teacher can listen.

688.text: A trustworthy messenger is honest, supported by good relationships, brave, and faithful to the message. A volunteer reporting a problem should tell the truth, seek the right support, and not be intimidated.

689.text: A messenger must deliver the ruler’s reply without letting fear make them add insulting or damaging words. Even under pressure, a spokesperson should repeat the agreed decision accurately.

690.text: A true messenger serves their ruler’s good without shrinking even when the duty is dangerous. Someone reporting a serious safety problem may risk criticism but must still speak up.

691.text: Those who work close to an unpredictable ruler should keep a careful middle distance, like someone warming by a fire. In a tense workplace, stay respectful without becoming so familiar that boundaries disappear.

692.text: A person serving a ruler should not chase the ruler’s favorite people or interests for personal gain; restraint can earn lasting trust and reward. An adviser who avoids flattering every favorite may be trusted with important work.

693.text: Protect yourself by avoiding serious mistakes; once a ruler suspects you, clearing the suspicion is very hard. A manager who hides one major error may lose trust even after explaining it later.

694.text: In the presence of a powerful leader, do not whisper to one person or share private laughter with another. During a formal meeting, speak openly and avoid side conversations that look disrespectful.

695.text: Do not listen in on a ruler’s private discussion or press for its contents; wait until it is shared with you. If classmates are having a confidential conversation, do not hover or demand to know.

696.text: Understand the leader’s mood, choose the right time, and present useful ideas in a way they can accept. Give feedback when your supervisor is ready to hear it, and frame it as a practical solution.

697.text: Offer useful advice, even when it is not requested, but do not recommend something merely because it is requested if it has no value. If a friend asks you to join a pointless argument, suggest a better use of your time.

698.text: Respect a ruler’s position instead of looking down on them because they are younger or related to you. A younger team captain still deserves respect for the responsibility they carry.

699.text: Clear judgment does not treat special favor as permission to do what the ruler dislikes. Being a trusted employee does not make it acceptable to ignore workplace rules.

700.text: Long familiarity is not a license to behave badly; using closeness as an excuse can lead to ruin. A longtime friend at work can still lose trust by abusing personal access.

701.text: A perceptive adviser can understand what someone means without being told, simply by noticing their face and behavior. If a teammate goes quiet and looks worried, noticing it early lets you offer help before they have to ask.

702.text: Someone who can understand another person's feelings clearly and without guesswork deserves extraordinary respect. A close friend who notices you are anxious even when you say 'I'm fine' shows this rare insight.

703.text: A person who can read unspoken signals is worth keeping as a trusted helper, whatever it costs. A team leader should value the colleague who senses confusion in a meeting and helps everyone get back on track.

704.text: People may look alike, but they differ greatly in their ability to understand what others mean without being told. In a group project, one student catches a partner's hesitation while another misses every hint.

705.text: Eyes are of little use if they cannot notice the meaning shown by another person's face and actions. Seeing a friend force a smile should prompt you to ask whether something is wrong.

706.text: Like a clear mirror, the face often reveals what is strongest in a person's mind. Someone nervous about a presentation may show it through tense expressions before saying a word.

707.text: The face often reveals liking or dislike before a person can explain it, making it a remarkably wise signal. A friend's face may light up at a surprise gift before they manage to say thank you.

708.text: When someone truly understands your inner state, you may not need to explain everything; your expression can be enough. A caring counselor may realize a student needs support from one glance and a quiet pause.

709.text: To someone skilled at reading eyes, a person's look can reveal friendship or hostility even when their words stay polite. During a new partnership, steady warmth or guarded suspicion may say more than the greeting.

710.text: For people who claim to understand subtle thoughts, the eyes are the measuring tool they rely on. An experienced interviewer may notice a candidate's eye movement and expression while listening, without treating one glance as proof.

711.text: People who understand language should first understand their audience and then choose their words carefully. Explaining a technical project to classmates, teachers, and visitors may require different levels of detail.

712.text: A wise speaker considers the setting, the listeners, and the right moment before speaking. In a meeting, waiting until the group is ready can make useful advice easier to hear.

713.text: Anyone who speaks without knowing the audience has not really learned how words work or how to use them well. A joke that fits a group chat can fail badly in a serious school meeting.

714.text: Show your full understanding among people who can appreciate it, but explain things simply to people who need a clearer starting point. A science student may discuss details with researchers and use an everyday example with a younger sibling.

715.text: Among people wiser than you, the best quality is the humility to listen instead of rushing to speak. In a class discussion, let the expert finish before adding your own point.

716.text: Making a serious mistake before people with deep knowledge can undo your standing, just as stumbling can take someone off a good path. Before presenting to a review panel, prepare carefully rather than guessing.

717.text: Learning truly shines when it is expressed clearly before people who can examine every word. A student's careful explanation stands out in a discussion where classmates ask thoughtful questions.

718.text: Speaking to people who are ready and able to understand is like watering a growing plant: the effort helps it flourish. A useful workshop becomes more valuable when participants are engaged and willing to learn.

719.text: Do not offer valuable guidance to an audience that only mocks or misuses it; even good words can be wasted there. If a group turns every thoughtful suggestion into a joke, save the advice for people ready to act on it.

720.text: Sharing a good idea with people who cannot value it is like pouring something precious onto dirty ground. Posting a thoughtful solution in a hostile comment thread may only invite abuse instead of helping anyone.

721.text: People who understand words and first read the audience can speak confidently without stumbling before powerful listeners. A new employee can present a well-prepared proposal calmly even when senior leaders are in the room.

722.text: Among learned people, the most respected are those who can present what they know in a way other learned people can understand and appreciate. A researcher who explains a complex result clearly earns both attention and useful questions.

723.text: Many people can face physical danger, but far fewer can speak without fear before an intelligent audience. Asking a difficult question in a packed seminar can require more courage than staying silent.

724.text: Share what you have learned clearly with knowledgeable people, then learn from those who know more than you. After presenting a project, a student should welcome a mentor's corrections instead of treating them as an insult.

725.text: Study sound reasoning and clear language so you can answer questions confidently in a public discussion. Knowing how to support a claim with evidence helps when classmates challenge your idea.

726.text: A weapon is useless in the hands of someone without courage, and learning is useless if fear keeps someone from speaking. A student may know the answer but gain no benefit from it by never raising a hand.

727.text: Knowledge kept silent before an audience is like a bright sword held by someone who will not face danger. A well-read employee who never shares a needed warning leaves the team unprotected.

728.text: Reading many books is not enough if you cannot communicate worthwhile ideas in a way good listeners can understand. A student may master the material yet fail to help the group if the explanation is confusing.

729.text: A person who has learned but is too afraid to speak before thoughtful people may be worse off than someone who never studied, because unused learning helps no one. An employee who knows how to fix a problem but hides during the review cannot contribute.

730.text: Someone who cannot share what they know meaningfully, because they fear the audience, is alive but contributes as little as the dead. A team member with the right solution adds nothing if they never speak up.

731.text: A good country brings together reliable food production, capable and honorable people, and wealth that is managed without decline. A healthy town has productive farms, trustworthy public servants, and businesses that create lasting value.

732.text: A strong country has abundant resources, attracts people, avoids serious ruin, and produces generously. A city with good jobs, fertile land, dependable services, and safe neighborhoods becomes a place where families want to live.

733.text: A good country can carry new burdens, such as welcoming displaced people, while still meeting its responsibilities to the government and community. When a disaster brings new families to a town, strong local resources let it provide shelter and keep essential services running.

734.text: A good country protects people from severe hunger, lasting disease, and destructive enemies. A community with affordable food, reliable healthcare, and public safety gives its people room to live and grow.

735.text: A good country is not torn apart by destructive factions, hidden internal sabotage, or violent gangs that threaten public life. A neighborhood becomes unsafe when rival groups undermine every shared project and intimidation replaces cooperation.

736.text: The best country resists harm and can recover without losing its ability to prosper. After a severe storm, a resilient town restores homes, jobs, and services instead of remaining broken.

737.text: A country's foundations include dependable water, useful high ground and natural resources, rainfall, and strong defenses. A town preparing for emergencies needs reservoirs, protected terrain, and secure shelters, not just buildings.

738.text: A country is adorned by five things: freedom from disease, material security, good production, people's happiness, and protection. A good neighborhood has healthcare, work, food, a joyful community life, and safety.

739.text: The best country has resources that sustain it naturally, rather than depending on endless hardship to produce every benefit. People value a place with reliable water, fertile land, and steady energy more than one where basic needs require constant struggle.

740.text: Even great resources are useless when a country lacks a government that serves its people well. A wealthy city can still fail if corrupt leadership leaves residents without fair services or trust.

741.text: A fort matters both to those who go out to face danger and to those who need a safe place to withstand it. An emergency operations center can support rescue teams outside while sheltering people inside.

742.text: A strong fort needs clear water, open ground, high terrain, and cool natural cover. A disaster shelter is more dependable when it has clean water, room to move, higher ground, and protection from heat.

743.text: A proper fort combines height, space, strength, and difficulty of access. A secure facility is safer when its walls are hard to reach, wide enough to operate in, and strong enough to withstand attack.

744.text: A good fort protects a small area while providing broad space inside and making attackers lose confidence. An emergency base works best when its vital rooms are easy to guard and its layout gives a threatening intruder no advantage.

745.text: A fort should be hard to capture, stocked with provisions, and arranged so those inside can hold their position. A shelter prepared for a long emergency needs food, water, and a layout that lets people protect and support one another.

746.text: A fort needs all essential supplies and capable people who can help defend it when danger comes. During a crisis, a community center is useful only if it has equipment and trained volunteers ready to act.

747.text: A strong fort must resist a blockade, a direct assault, and schemes from within. A well-protected emergency base needs plans for outside attack, prolonged isolation, and betrayal from inside.

748.text: A fort proves its strength when its defenders hold their ground and overcome even a stronger force outside. A smaller emergency team can protect a shelter if it stays organized instead of abandoning its position in panic.

749.text: A fort is truly excellent when the people inside can use wise tactics to defeat attackers at the point of danger. A trained rescue and security team may protect a facility by responding strategically rather than reacting blindly.

750.text: Even the strongest structure is useless if the people responsible for it cannot act well. Resources and good planning need capable people to turn them into protection and results. For example, a school may have excellent buildings and technology, but it will not help students if its staff cannot organize lessons and respond to problems effectively.

751.text: Wealth can make even a person whom society ignores seem important. This warns us that people are often judged by money rather than character. For example, someone may suddenly receive respect after getting a high-paying job, even if their values have not changed.

752.text: People often look down on those without money and praise those who have it. Valluvar points out this unfair habit, not that it is right. For example, a student from a poor family may be overlooked while a wealthy student is given extra attention.

753.text: Wealth can act like a light that helps a person reach distant places and remove obstacles, including hostility. It gives influence beyond one's immediate surroundings. For example, funding can help a community take its needs to decision-makers and build support for a solution.

754.text: Wealth earned through fair work and without harming others can support both a good life and happiness. The way money is gained matters as much as the money itself. For example, an honest business can pay its workers fairly and still give its owner a secure life.

755.text: Do not seek wealth that is built without compassion or love. Money gained by exploiting people may look successful, but it is not worth embracing. For example, a company should reject profits that depend on unsafe work or cheating customers.

756.text: A ruler's resources may come from lawful revenue such as taxes, customs, unclaimed property, and payments from defeated enemies. The couplet describes the main sources that supported a kingdom. In modern life, a public budget likewise depends on collecting and managing shared revenue responsibly.

757.text: Compassion is born from love, but it needs resources to grow and reach people. Wealth can support kindness when it is used well. For example, a caring person can turn concern for hungry families into meals, shelter, or practical help.

758.text: Starting a task with resources already in hand is like watching a difficult contest from a safe hill: it gives confidence and control. Preparation makes hard work less dangerous. For example, a student with savings and a clear plan can begin a course without being overwhelmed by every expense.

759.text: Build legitimate resources, because strength and independence can restrain an opponent's arrogance. Valluvar presents wealth as a sharper tool than force alone. For example, a financially stable organization can refuse unfair pressure instead of accepting every demand.

760.text: People who gain abundant wealth by honorable means can more easily pursue virtue and a satisfying life. Good resources create room to help others and live with less fear. For example, a stable income can let someone support family members, give to a cause, and still rest peacefully.

761.text: A ruler's greatest resource is a complete, disciplined force that can face danger without losing courage. Strength depends on readiness, not just numbers. For example, an emergency team is valuable when it has the right skills, equipment, and calm people ready to act.

762.text: A long-established force shows its deepest courage when it stands by its leader even after suffering losses. Loyalty is tested when success is no longer certain. For example, an experienced rescue crew may keep helping during a failed operation instead of abandoning the people who depend on it.

763.text: A loud crowd is not necessarily a strong one; many fearful people can be overcome by a smaller group with real courage and discipline. Noise alone does not create power. For example, a large online campaign may achieve little when a small, well-prepared team calmly addresses the real issue.

764.text: A true force remains steady, avoids being destroyed, and does not betray its side through fear or deceit. Endurance and trust are part of strength. For example, a crisis team earns confidence when it keeps its promises and protects sensitive work under pressure.

765.text: A real force can unite and stand firm even when the danger seems overwhelming. Courage is stronger when people do not face fear alone. For example, a team handling a serious emergency can stay effective by sharing responsibility instead of each person panicking separately.

766.text: An effective force needs four safeguards: courage, honor, a worthy tradition of conduct, and the leader's trust. Skill without character is not enough. For example, a project team works best when its members are brave about problems, ethical, well trained, and trusted with responsibility.

767.text: A strong force understands how to meet the first attack and can withstand the pressure that comes with it. Readiness matters before the struggle begins. For example, a school debate team that studies likely questions can stay composed when difficult challenges come first.

768.text: A force may look impressive even when it lacks the courage and strength needed for real action, but appearance alone cannot produce lasting success. Presentation is not performance. For example, a beautifully designed project will still fail if the team has not tested whether it works.

769.text: A force can win when it does not keep shrinking, turn against its leader, or suffer from a lack of resources. Unity, loyalty, and support must remain intact. For example, a volunteer group is more likely to finish its work when people stay committed and basic supplies are available.

770.text: Even a large group of steady soldiers cannot last without capable leaders. Numbers need direction and coordination. For example, a workplace may have many talented employees, but a project can still collapse if nobody makes clear decisions.

771.text: The warrior warns enemies that many who challenged his leader ended as memorial stones. The image stresses the danger of reckless pride in battle. For example, someone should not provoke a proven expert merely to show off without understanding the consequences.

772.text: A brave attempt at a great challenge can be more honorable than an easy success with a small goal. The value lies in the courage and ambition behind the effort. For example, applying for a demanding scholarship and missing it can teach more than choosing a competition that offers no real challenge.

773.text: Bravery is not only the power to face an enemy; its highest form is helping that enemy when misfortune strikes. Strength can make room for mercy. For example, after defeating a rival team, a captain can still help an injured opponent get medical care.

774.text: The warrior who has used his weapon keeps fighting by pulling another from his own wound. The image praises fierce resilience in the face of pain. For example, after a serious setback, a determined person may recover, learn from it, and return to finish an important responsibility.

775.text: A warrior who claims courage should not lose heart at the first weapon thrown by an opponent. The couplet treats even a moment of flinching as a failure of resolve. For example, someone who accepts a difficult role should not abandon it as soon as criticism appears.

776.text: The warrior counts days without a battle wound as days that did not fully serve his purpose. This reflects the extreme warrior ideal of proving courage through sacrifice. For example, a person devoted to public service may feel that time matters most when it is spent facing real problems rather than seeking comfort.

777.text: Some warriors value a lasting reputation more than their own safety, and wearing the warrior's anklet becomes a sign of that dedication. The couplet praises commitment to a cause larger than oneself. For example, a volunteer may accept difficult, unseen work because its lasting benefit matters more than personal attention.

778.text: A fearless warrior does not lose his courage when danger comes, even if a ruler tries to hold him back. The couplet celebrates steadfast commitment to duty. For example, a trained caregiver may remain ready to help during a crisis, while still following lawful and responsible instructions.

779.text: Who can call a person a failure when that person dies while keeping a sworn promise? The couplet honors faithfulness to one's word, especially under extreme pressure. For example, a teammate who completes a serious commitment despite hardship earns respect even if the final result is imperfect.

780.text: A warrior's death is described as especially honored when it moves the ruler who was protected by that sacrifice. The point is that devoted service can leave a lasting mark on those who benefited from it. For example, a community may remember a responder who gave everything to keep others safe.

781.text: True friendship is difficult to gain, and once gained it becomes a strong protection that is hard to break. A loyal friend is both a rare treasure and a source of safety. For example, a dependable friend can stand beside you when rumors or pressure try to isolate you.

782.text: The friendship of wise people grows like the waxing moon, while the friendship of foolish people fades like the waning moon. Good judgment gives a relationship room to deepen. For example, a friend who listens and learns with you may become closer over the years, while a careless friendship may disappear after its first excitement.

783.text: Friendship with a person of good character becomes more enjoyable the more you share it, just as a good book reveals more each time you read it. Time brings out its value. For example, studying, working, or volunteering together can show new strengths in a friend year after year.

784.text: Friendship is not only for laughing together; a true friend also steps forward to correct you when you go too far. Honest advice protects the relationship from becoming harmful. For example, a friend may tell you to stop cheating or insulting someone even when hearing it is uncomfortable.

785.text: People do not need to live together or meet constantly to become true friends. Mutual understanding can create closeness on its own. For example, two students who support each other online and share the same values may form a real friendship despite living far apart.

786.text: A friendly smile alone is not proof of friendship. True friendship comes from genuine care in the heart, not just pleasant behavior in public. For example, someone who checks on you privately when you are struggling is a truer friend than someone who only acts warm in front of others.

787.text: A true friend turns you away from harmful choices, guides you toward a better path, and shares your pain when trouble arrives. Friendship includes both correction and support. For example, a friend might stop you from making a reckless decision and then stay with you while you repair the damage.

788.text: A true friend removes trouble immediately, like a hand that instinctively fixes a loosened garment before others notice. Help should come quickly when a friend is in need. For example, a friend may call for help and take charge at once when you suddenly fall ill in public.

789.text: Friendship is at its best when people support each other steadily, without needless division, whenever they are able. Reliability gives friendship its strength. For example, close friends keep showing up for one another during exams, unemployment, illness, or other difficult seasons.

790.text: Friendship becomes shallow when people keep decorating it with claims about how close they are. Real closeness does not need repeated public praise. For example, friends who constantly post about their bond may be less dependable than the quiet friend who simply helps when needed.

791.text: Because kind-hearted people may not easily abandon someone they have accepted, choosing a friend without careful thought can bring great harm. It is wiser to examine a relationship before becoming deeply tied to it. For example, notice how someone treats others before trusting them with personal matters.

792.text: A friendship chosen without repeated care and judgment can eventually cause deep suffering. First impressions are not enough for a close bond. For example, ignoring a person's repeated dishonesty may later leave you responsible for debts or damage caused by their choices.

793.text: Before forming a close friendship, look at a person's character, habits, faults, background, and the people around them. Understanding the whole pattern is wiser than judging one charming moment. For example, notice whether a new friend is honest with family, classmates, and strangers alike.

794.text: A person with good values who feels ashamed of doing wrong is worth making a real effort to befriend. A sense of responsibility is a sign of trustworthy character. For example, a colleague who admits a mistake and works to fix it may be worth keeping close, even if earning their trust takes time.

795.text: Choose friends who can warn you before you do wrong, correct you afterward, and understand how life works. Their advice may hurt, but it protects you. For example, a good friend will challenge a dishonest plan instead of cheering you on just to stay popular.

796.text: Hard times contain one useful lesson: they reveal who your real friends are. Trouble measures loyalty more clearly than easy days do. For example, when a family faces sudden financial difficulty, the people who offer practical help show the depth of their care.

797.text: Leaving the friendship of foolish people can itself be a gain. A harmful companion can waste judgment, time, and opportunity. For example, stepping away from friends who pressure you into reckless behavior can improve your studies, health, and future.

798.text: Do not fill your mind with choices that destroy your courage, and do not choose friends who will leave you in trouble. Both discouraging thoughts and unreliable companions weaken you. For example, before joining a risky venture, ask whether the people involved will still stand by you when it becomes difficult.

799.text: When people abandon us in our worst hour, remembering that betrayal can hurt even long afterward. A friendship that disappears in crisis leaves a lasting wound. For example, someone may remember for years the friend who walked away when help was urgently needed.

800.text: Stay close to people who are sincere and free from harmful motives, and leave relationships with people whose values repeatedly conflict with what is right. A clean friendship is worth protecting, while a damaging one may be worth ending at a cost. For example, it can be wiser to leave a dishonest group than to keep belonging at the price of your integrity.

801.text: Long friendship allows trusted friends to act with familiar freedom without destroying the bond. If a longtime friend makes a small mistake while trying to help, do not treat it as betrayal.

802.text: A friend's freedom to act openly is part of real friendship, and accepting it shows maturity. If a close friend changes a shared plan to help, appreciate the trust behind the gesture.

803.text: Long friendship means standing by a trusted friend's action as you would stand by your own, when it was done in good faith. If a longtime friend handles a shared task without asking first, support the effort unless it causes real harm.

804.text: When a trusted friend acts without asking out of familiarity, a wise person values the goodwill if the action is helpful. If a friend submits something on your behalf to meet a deadline, thank them instead of taking offense.

805.text: When a friend does something hurtful, it may come from ignorance or from feeling close enough to act freely. Before ending the friendship over a mistake, ask whether they misunderstood or assumed your trust.

806.text: A person who understands true friendship does not abandon a longtime friend just because the relationship has become difficult. When a friend loses a job or faces a crisis, stay supportive instead of disappearing.

807.text: A bond rooted in love is not thrown away just because a friend makes a damaging mistake. If a close friend gives bad advice that costs you an opportunity, address the mistake without erasing your care for them.

808.text: Loyalty should not mean ignoring every warning about a friend; if that friend abuses such trust, the friendship has been wasted. If several people point out repeated cheating, do not call it loyalty to pretend nothing is wrong.

809.text: People respect those who do not abandon a longtime friend when circumstances change. If a friend moves away or struggles financially, keep in touch instead of remembering them only when life is easy.

810.text: Even opponents respect someone who remains steady in affection for longtime friends. A rival may still admire you for giving an old friend a fair chance when others turn against them.

811.text: It is better to reduce contact with someone who acts loving but lacks good character than to let that friendship grow. If a classmate flatters you while pressuring you to cheat, create some distance.

812.text: There is little value in a friendship that lasts only while someone is gaining from it. If a person messages you only before exams or when they need money, losing that contact is not a real loss.

813.text: A friendship measured only by profit is just a transaction, no more honorable than a deal driven by payment or theft. If someone joins your group only for rewards and leaves when work begins, do not mistake that for friendship.

814.text: Being alone is better than relying on people who abandon you when you need them, like an untrained horse throwing its rider. If a teammate disappears before every deadline, working alone may be safer than depending on them.

815.text: It is better to avoid the friendship of people who cannot protect or support you even after promising to do so. If someone agrees to keep a confidence but immediately shares it, do not entrust them with another one.

816.text: The opposition of a wise person can help more than the close friendship of a fool. A thoughtful critic who challenges your plan may do you more good than a reckless friend who always agrees.

817.text: A rival's honest criticism can help more than the friendship of people who only joke and never truly care. If a teammate points out a serious flaw, value that help over empty laughter from a cheerful group.

818.text: Gradually step back from people who pretend they cannot help and then spoil work they could have done. If a teammate repeatedly avoids their part and causes missed deadlines, stop giving them important tasks.

819.text: A friendship is deeply troubling when a person's actions never match their promises. If a friend repeatedly says they will support you but abandons you, the uncertainty can follow you even when you are trying to rest.

820.text: Keep your distance from people who are warm in private but ridicule you in public. If a classmate is kind when you are alone but mocks you in a group, that is not a friendship to protect.

821.text: A person who pretends to be your friend without caring about you may turn that closeness into a weapon when an opportunity appears. If a coworker collects personal information while acting close, be careful about what you share.

822.text: People who only seem like friends may change their attitude whenever it suits them, showing one face outside and another inside. If someone is warm until a more popular group arrives, recognize that the friendship is unstable.

823.text: Reading many good books does not make a hostile person kind-hearted; knowledge without goodwill does not create true friendship. Someone can quote lessons about kindness while still hoping others fail.

824.text: Be cautious of a deceitful person who smiles warmly while secretly wishing you harm. If someone praises your work but quietly tries to sabotage it, trust their pattern of actions rather than their smile.

825.text: Do not rely on the words of someone whose heart is not with you. If a teammate promises to help but repeatedly works against the plan, verify their commitments and prepare another option.

826.text: An enemy may speak kindly like a friend, but hidden hostility usually shows itself soon. If a rival offers advice that conveniently harms your work, check the facts and the motive before accepting it.

827.text: Do not mistake an enemy's polite words for goodwill; a bow bends because it is ready to send an arrow. When a competitor suddenly praises your proposal while looking for weaknesses, stay courteous but cautious.

828.text: A hostile person may hide danger behind a respectful gesture, and even tears may be part of a plan. If someone apologizes dramatically while preparing to retaliate, judge their actions and protect yourself.

829.text: When people pretend to care while secretly despising you, stay calm and polite without giving them your trust, and let the false friendship fade. If a club member smiles at you but mocks you privately, keep the peace and stop sharing personal matters.

830.text: When an enemy begins acting like a friend, be courteous in public without giving your inner trust until their change is proven. If a former rival joins your project, cooperate professionally but do not share sensitive information too soon.

831.text: Foolishness is choosing what harms you while giving up what would help you. A student who spends needed savings on a risky shortcut may lose both the money and the chance to prepare properly.

832.text: The greatest foolishness is taking pleasure in doing what is wrong or not suited to you. Someone who chases online attention by humiliating another person may enjoy the moment and regret the damage later.

833.text: A fool is unashamed of wrongdoing, ignores what is worth seeking, lacks kindness, and protects nothing valuable. Someone who will not apologize, learn, care for others, or keep a promise shows all four habits.

834.text: No one is more foolish than a person who studies good principles, teaches them to others, and then refuses to live by them. A student who lectures classmates about honesty while cheating has learned words, not wisdom.

835.text: One reckless choice can create suffering that lasts for years, as if a person had built their own prison. A careless post that destroys trust can close doors long after the original moment has passed.

836.text: A person who takes on work without knowing how to do it may fail and then face serious consequences. If someone accepts a technical task without learning or asking for help, the project and their own reputation may suffer.

837.text: When a foolish person gains great wealth, outsiders may enjoy it while the people who depend on them go without. Someone who spends family savings impressing new friends may leave their own household struggling.

838.text: When a foolish person suddenly gains money or power, the result can be like giving alcohol to someone already dizzy. An immature person with new authority may become reckless instead of using it responsibly.

839.text: The friendship of fools is easy to leave because neither person has built anything worth missing. Two unreliable friends may drift apart after a shallow shared interest, and neither feels much pain.

840.text: A person who enters a thoughtful gathering without basic respect or preparation can disturb it like unwashed feet on a clean bed. Someone who interrupts a serious discussion with loud, uninformed claims makes the whole group uncomfortable.

841.text: Lack of wisdom is the greatest kind of poverty; lacking money is less serious if good judgment remains. A person with few resources can rebuild, while a wealthy person without wisdom can ruin everything.

842.text: When a foolish person gives something generously, the good fortune belongs more to the receiver than to the giver's judgment. If a careless person unexpectedly shares a useful opportunity, be grateful without assuming they will act wisely every time.

843.text: Foolish people can cause themselves suffering that even their enemies could hardly cause. Someone who ignores every warning and repeats the same harmful choices may hurt their future more than any rival could.

844.text: Ignorance is not merely lacking knowledge; it is the arrogance of claiming to be wise. Someone who refuses to ask questions because they must look smartest is showing that very ignorance.

845.text: Pretending to know what you have not learned can make people doubt even the things you truly understand. If a student fakes expertise in a new subject, classmates may question their genuine work too.

846.text: It is foolish to hide your outward faults while refusing to correct the faults that cause real harm. Editing a perfect apology or public image means little if you keep repeating the same behavior.

847.text: A person who ignores valuable advice causes great harm to themselves. If a mentor warns you about a scam and you refuse to listen, the loss that follows is largely your own making.

848.text: A person who follows neither good advice nor their own careful thinking remains a burden to everyone around them. If a team member ignores instructions and never learns, others must keep redoing their work.

849.text: Trying to teach someone who refuses to see evidence can expose the teacher's own foolishness, while the stubborn person still believes they are wise. An endless online argument may drain your time without changing a mind closed to facts.

850.text: A person who deliberately denies a truth supported by clear evidence may be treated as an outcast for rejecting what wiser people can see. Someone who dismisses a verified safety rule just to appear clever puts everyone at risk.

851.text: Hatred is a sickness that breaks people's bonds and keeps them from living together. For example, a team falls apart when members treat every disagreement as a personal fight.

852.text: Even when someone treats you badly because of a disagreement, do not hurt that person in return. For example, answer a rude classmate calmly instead of spreading a rumor about them.

853.text: When a person removes hatred from the heart, a lasting and honorable reputation can grow. For example, forgiving a former teammate can earn more respect than winning an argument.

854.text: Letting go of hatred removes the deepest kind of pain and opens the way to the deepest joy. For example, making peace with a family member can bring relief that revenge never could.

855.text: People who refuse to let hatred control them are not easily defeated. For example, someone who stays calm when provoked online keeps control of the situation.

856.text: Anyone who thinks hatred is a pleasant way to win is moving quickly toward failure and ruin. For example, a long feud at work can cost a person both trust and opportunities.

857.text: Hatred clouds judgment, so a person ruled by it cannot see the truth that leads to real success. For example, a manager who dislikes an employee may ignore the best idea in the room.

858.text: Turning away from hatred brings strength and benefit, while feeding it invites trouble and ruin. For example, choosing a fair solution in a dispute protects a project better than keeping the conflict alive.

859.text: When good fortune is approaching, a wise person does not nurture resentment; someone seeking ruin makes every grievance bigger. For example, one small mistake need not destroy a promising partnership.

860.text: Hatred brings many troubles, while friendly cooperation brings the happiness and goodness of a strong community. For example, neighbors who work together solve problems that constant arguments only worsen.

861.text: In a conflict, do not recklessly challenge someone stronger, and do not let a weaker aggressor cause harm without response. For example, choose a safe, fair way to handle a dispute instead of provoking a powerful rival or bullying an easier target.

862.text: A person who lacks love, dependable allies, and personal strength cannot easily overcome an enemy. For example, a project leader who has lost the team's trust will struggle when a serious problem appears.

863.text: A fearful, ignorant, uncooperative, and ungenerous person becomes an easy target for opponents. For example, a leader who refuses advice and never helps others will quickly lose support in a crisis.

864.text: Someone who cannot control anger or keep a steady mind is easy for others to defeat at any time. For example, a person who reveals private plans during every outburst gives rivals an advantage.

865.text: A person who ignores the right path, fails to do what fits the situation, fears no blame, and lacks good character becomes easy for enemies to overcome. For example, a careless leader who breaks promises soon loses both trust and protection.

866.text: Blind anger and uncontrolled desire make a person's hostility easy for others to face. For example, a rival who lashes out without checking the facts can be guided into making a damaging mistake.

867.text: When someone close to a shared task keeps acting against its purpose, it may be necessary to treat that opposition openly, even at a cost. For example, a team may have to end a partnership with a member who repeatedly sabotages its work.

868.text: A person with no good qualities and many faults loses allies, and that loss strengthens the enemy. For example, a dishonest leader may find that former supporters leave just when the organization is under pressure.

869.text: When opponents are both ignorant and fearful, success is less difficult and good opportunities stay within reach. For example, a well-prepared team has an easier contest when its rival panics and refuses to learn.

870.text: A person who will not stand up even to an unskilled opponent will never gain a reputation for courage. For example, someone who avoids every reasonable challenge will not be trusted with a difficult responsibility.

871.text: Hatred is so harmful that it should not be welcomed even as a joke or a game. For example, playful insults in a group chat can become real hostility when people keep repeating them.

872.text: You may have to face a warrior's hostility, but do not needlessly make an enemy of a skilled speaker or writer. For example, a thoughtful critic can influence many people with a few well-chosen words.

873.text: A person who stands alone while making enemies of many people is more foolish than someone who has lost good judgment. For example, a leader who insults every partner soon has no one left to help.

874.text: The world respects the greatness of a good-natured person who knows how to turn hostility into friendship. For example, a mediator who helps two rival groups cooperate earns trust from both sides.

875.text: When you are alone, without allies, and surrounded by two opponents, turn one of them into a friendly ally. For example, two competing teams may resolve their differences so they can face a larger problem together.

876.text: In a crisis, even if you know someone is an enemy, do not rush into close alliance or open separation; keep a careful balance. For example, cooperate with a rival during an emergency while protecting your own team's interests.

877.text: Do not announce your suffering to people who do not understand it, and do not display your weakness before enemies. For example, share a workplace problem with a trusted adviser rather than posting every detail publicly.

878.text: Know how to act, strengthen yourself, and protect your position; then an enemy's pride will fade. For example, a prepared team with clear plans and reliable support can quiet a rival's confidence.

879.text: Deal with a growing threat while it is still small; once it grows, removing it can hurt the person who tries. For example, report repeated harassment early instead of waiting until it damages the whole group.

880.text: If you cannot stop a determined enemy from causing harm, your safety may not last. For example, a serious security flaw left unchecked can eventually bring down an entire service.
